native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: The simultaneous collapse of Diversity in Pottery Form and increase in Diversity in Pottery Decoration occurs in the 17th century BCE (~1700 BCE), at the Late Neolithic to Older Bronze Age transition: Pottery Form diversity drops from +0.74 to its series minimum -1.13 (delta -1.87, ~3.4 sigma) while Pottery Decoration diversity simultaneously rises from -0.48 to +0.97 (delta +1.45, ~3.5 sigma) in the 100-year bin centered on 1700 BCE. This is the only century in the record where a large Form collapse coincides with a large Decoration increase; Form remains at its minimum and Decoration stays elevated thereafter (reaching +1.53 from 1000 BCE). Contextually, this cultural reversal precedes the strong rise in land-use openness and demographic expansion visible from ~1400 BCE onward, suggesting a cultural reorganization at the LN-OBA transition rather than an immediate response to an openness or demographic spike.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded time_series_data.csv (3601 annual rows CE -4100..-500) and capital.csv (39 century rows BCE 4300..500, comma decimals); verified ZKeform/Zkeverz are identical to raw PotteryForm/PotteryDecoration (max abs diff 0.0). 2) Raw pottery values exist only at 37 century markers, so analysis is at century (100-year bin) level, matching the study's 100-year binning; _inter columns are linear interpolations and were used only as a robustness check. 3) Computed century-to-century first differences (sigma(dPF)=0.546, sigma(dPD)=0.420) and systematically searched for simultaneous events (dPF <= -k*sigma AND dPD >= +k*sigma) at k=1.0, 1.5, 2.0: only BCE 1700 qualifies under all thresholds, including when additionally requiring PF to reach the series minimum. 4) Secondary candidates (4000, 2800, 2400, 1000 BCE) fail the simultaneous opposite-direction requirement. 5) Quantified the 1700 BCE transition (before/after z-values and deltas); the _inter century-mean check smears the step over 1700/1600 bins, confirming the step lands at the 1700 BCE marker. 6) Added contextual pollen openness (SMOOTH_MEAN_100y) and KDE demographic series around the transition, explicitly labeled as context only.

native_result.query: How were the phases of the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE) characterized in terms of the first principal component in a PCA on the forms of capital analyzed in hundred-year time slices?
native_result.HypoA: During the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE), both phases are primarily associated with negative values on the first principal component (PC1). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB:
RESULT — PCA on the 12 forms of capital (capital.csv, 39 hundred-year bins, BCE 4300–500), 12 Z columns re-standardized, PC1 extracted with sign convention "ZMonument (monument count) loading positive".

METHOD/WORKFLOW (executed): loaded capital.csv with decimal=',' (German commas), dropped group/color; verified 0 missing values; re-standardized the 12 Z variables across the 39 rows; ran correlation-matrix PCA (NumPy SVD, n=39 × p=12); extracted PC1 scores per 100-year bin; characterized the two target phases (endpoints included); ran two robustness checks and a supplementary pollen comparison. Script: analysis_capital_pca.py; outputs: outputs/pc1_scores_by_century.csv, outputs/pc1_loadings.csv.

PC1 STRUCTURE (observed): PC1 explains 30.3% of variance (PC2 19.5%). With the stated sign convention, the POSITIVE pole is dominated by copper/gold (ZCU_AU +0.41), pottery decoration (Zkeverz +0.38), hoards/deposits (ZHort +0.34) and hatchets/swords (ZAxtSchwert +0.30); the NEGATIVE pole by pottery form (ZKeform −0.35), axes/celts (ZBeil −0.24) and amber (Zamber −0.24); monument count (+0.20) and monument size (+0.24) sit mildly positive. Across the full 4300–500 BCE series PC1 rises from ≈ −1.7/−2.0 (Early Neolithic) to ≈ +3.1 (OBA) and +1.8 (YBA) — i.e., PC1 broadly tracks long-term growth of metal-prestige/hoard-type capital.

PHASE CHARACTERIZATIONS (observed PCA results):
• Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE, group MN): mean PC1 = −1.37 (sd 0.49), well below the full-series mean (0 by construction; full-series sd 1.91). Within-phase trend is NEGATIVE: OLS slope −0.26 per 100-y step, falling from −0.58 (3400 BCE) to −1.78 (3000 BCE), the phase minimum.
• Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE, group SG): mean PC1 = −1.12 (sd 0.43), slightly higher than the Middle Neolithic (difference +0.26), still on the negative side. Within-phase trend is POSITIVE: slope +0.12 per 100-y step, rising from −1.50 (2900 BCE) to −0.41 (2300 BCE), the phase maximum.
• Phase ranking over all six groups (low→high PC1): EN (−1.74) < MN (−1.37) < YN/SG (−1.12) < LN (+0.33) < YBA (+1.85) < OBA (+3.09).

HYPOTHESIS (natural-language answer to the question): In a PCA of the twelve forms of capital in hundred-year time slices, the first principal component (~30% of variance) contrasts prestige-metal capital — copper/gold, hoards/deposits, and decorated pottery (plus, weakly, monument count/size) — against pottery form, axes/celts and amber. Both target phases lie on the negative (low) side of this axis. The Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE) is characterized by the lowest and steadily declining PC1 of any post-EN phase (mean −1.37, falling from −0.58 to −1.78): low expression of metal-prestige, hoard and pottery-decoration capital combined with comparatively high pottery-form values. The Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE) remains at a similarly low level (mean −1.12) but reverses the trend, with PC1 rising through the phase to −0.41 at 2300 BCE — the first sign of the recovery that accelerates through the Late Neolithic and peaks in the Older Bronze Age. Interpretation (distinct from the observed scores): the two Neolithic phases are thus jointly characterized by weak monetizable/prestige capital relative to the Bronze Age, with the Middle Neolithic marking a within-phase decline and the Younger Neolithic a modest, sustained upswing; supplementary pollen-openness data (Belau/Woserin) show nearly identical mean openness in both phases (MEAN −0.67 vs −0.66; 100-y smoothed −0.53 vs −0.57), consistent with no major openness-driven discontinuity between the phases — context only, not part of the PCA.

ROBUSTNESS NOTES (demoted per instruction): (1) Removing ZSichel (whose long run of exact zeros pre-2300 BCE could be structural) leaves PC1 essentially unchanged (EVR 32.6%; MN −1.44, YN −1.20; r = 0.996 with main PC1). (2) The raw century-point Z values in time_series_data.csv are numerically identical to capital.csv (all 12 variables, exact match), so using capital.csv vs. the time-series raw columns is equivalent; _inter columns simply interpolate between the same century points and were not needed.

LIMITATIONS: PC1 sign is arbitrary (convention stated above); re-standardizing the already Z-scaled columns is a modeling choice (results are near-identical without it, as the robustness check shows); ZSichel zeros may be absence-of-data rather than true zeros (checked, immaterial); 39 samples with piecewise-constant century values limit fine-grained trend inference; pollen PC1 is supplementary context only and does not enter the PCA.

native_result.query: Between 3400 BCE to 3000 BCE, how does the number of monuments and axes changes with elements of symbolic capital?
native_result.HypoA: Between 3400 BCE to 3000 BCE, the number of monuments and axes increases along with symbolic capital
native_result.HypoB: Between 3400 and 3000 BCE, monument construction and axe/celt activity form a single mid-window 'communal pulse' decoupled from symbolic and wealth capital: MonumentCount rises from z=-0.46 (3400 BCE) to a peak of z=+0.91 at 3200 BCE - exactly coinciding with the sharp AxesCelts spike to z=+2.60 - then falls back to z=-0.36 by 3000 BCE, while HouseSize declines monotonically from z=+2.05 to ~0 (trend r=-0.89) and correlates negatively with both MonumentCount (-0.35 anchors / -0.40 annual) and AxesCelts; the prestige objects defining symbolic capital stay flat (HatchetSword ~ -0.43, correlation with MonumentCount only ~ +0.28; Dagger constant at -0.58, relationship undefined). Secondary social-capital indices co-move inversely with the surge (CopperGold r = -0.54 to -0.65; Amber nominally positive but nearly constant). Pollen-based land openness declines steadily across the window (anchor-interpolated +1.65 to -1.16; pollen-file SMOOTH_MEAN_100y +0.20 to -1.81) and shows no positive association with the monument/axes pulse (MonumentCount~pollen r ~ 0; AxesCelts~pollen -0.22 to -0.67). Net: as land openness and household size wane, communal monumental effort and axe deposition surge once, peak together at 3200 BCE, and collapse by 3000 BCE - a shift from household/wealth display toward monumental display not driven by agricultural expansion. Descriptive/correlational only (5 independent 100-year bins; the 3200 BCE spike drives much of the trend); no causal claim is made.

native_result.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening varies strongly with habitat type in the Barcelona province: gardening aliens are most prevalent in absolute per-plot frequency in Coastal (0.79/plot), Wetland (0.76/plot) and Urban (0.69/plot) plots — statistically indistinguishable from one another — and constitute the majority share of the non-native flora in Wetlands (56%) and Coastal habitats (54%), rising to 87–100% in forest plots (low-confidence, few records). In contrast, Croplands (19% gardening share, 0.22/plot), Meadows, Scrublands and Rock outcrops are dominated by unintentionally introduced species and host few gardening aliens. This habitat effect persists after adjustment for elevation, climate, urban/cropland cover and distances (habitat-block LR p≈1e-12), and is consistent with the regional trend of gardening becoming the dominant introduction pathway (17% of introductions before 1500 vs 75% in 1985–2019).
native_result.WorkflowB: Read tab-separated invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots); verified count identity and zero missing values; computed per-habitat prop_gard = sum(n.gard)/sum(n.total) with Wilson 95% CIs and mean n.gard/plot; chi-square test on 10x2 gardening-vs-other table; binomial GLM cbind(n.gard, n.total-n.gard) ~ habitat on 191 invaded plots with marginal means and contrasts (Urban reference); Poisson GLM n.gard ~ habitat on all 632 plots (dispersion 1.14) with rate ratios; covariate-adjusted sensitivity models (elevation, annual temperature/rainfall, urban/cropland 2009 at 1000 m, distances to road/stream) plus landscape-change robustness and a crude spatial autocorrelation check; temporal contingency table (chi-square across periods) and deduplicated species-level pathway shares used as framing context.

native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants shows different prevalence styles across habitat types: it is proportionally dominant in natural/semi-natural and coastal-wetland habitats — in forests gardening species constitute nearly the entire alien flora (100% in broad-leaved, 88% in coniferous; low-evidence) and in wetlands and coastal habitats it is the leading pathway (~55% of alien records, present in ~45-50% of plots; both significantly more gardening-dominated than other high-evidence habitats, p=6.3e-04 and 6.7e-03) — whereas in the most human-modified, alien-rich habitats (urban, croplands) gardening is a minority share (29% and 19%) despite being frequently present (~48% of urban plots), because unintentional introductions dominate there (69-77% of records; croplands significantly gardening-poor, p=2.2e-04). Habitat x pathway composition differs highly significantly (pooled chi-square 66.20, df=12, p=1.6e-09; permutation p=5e-05). This pattern aligns with the regional temporal trend in which gardening became the dominant introduction pathway over time (share of first records 17% before 1500 to 75% in 1985-2019), suggesting gardening prevails as the introducer of aliens in natural/coastal-wetland contexts while unintentional introductions prevail in urban and agricultural contexts.

Built habitat x pathway contingency table (10 habitats x 3 pathways). Computed per-habitat prevalence styles: gardening share of alien records, per-plot mean gardening count (all plots as denominator incl. n.total=0), per-plot gardening presence frequency, and dominant pathway. Tested composition differences with chi-square after pooling habitats with <10 alien records (Coniferous, Broad-leaved, Scrublands, Rock outcrops), cross-checked with a 20,000-permutation exact test on fixed margins; pairwise 2xK chi-squares for high-evidence habitats. Caveats documented: counting semantics (species vs occurrences, possible multi-pathway assignment) undocumented; zero-alien plots assumed true absences; small-cell habitats marked low-evidence and excluded from the primary claim.

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted invasion by unintentionally introduced non-native plants (contaminant/stowaway introductions of global trade) specifically in landscapes that recently urbanized at the surrounding-landscape scale — plots whose 1000 m buffer gained substantial urban cover between 1993 and 2009 — where such species come to dominate the non-native flora (~78% of records vs ~52% in unchanged plots) and, region-wide, prove the most successful invaders (≈2.4× more invaded plots and larger area of occupancy than gardening- or agri-forest-introduced species even after accounting for residence time). Gardening-introduced ornamentals, despite dominating recent introductions overall (75% of 1985-2019 introductions), did not increase with urban land cover, and agriculture/forestry introductions were marginally suppressed in highly urban landscapes.
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspection and integrity checks (verified n.total = n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo; complete phylo tip matching incl. '2'-suffix duplicates; tab-delimited parsing), temporal chi-square on the 4×3 period×pathway table; species-level negative-binomial GLMs of invasion success (number.of.invaded.plots, area.of.occupancy.10km) on pathway with mrt adjustment after deduplication (one row per species; duplicated pairs verified identical); plot-level composition models on the 191 invaded plots: per-pathway negative-binomial GLMs with log(n.total) offset testing pathway×urban interactions for urban cover 2009 (50/1000 m) and urban-specific change deltas (1956→2009, 1993→2009; 50/1000 m) adjusted for habitat, elevation, temperature and rainfall, with urban-specific deltas as primary change predictors and the original mixed 'progressive' columns as sensitivity checks; sensitivity analyses excluding the 4 anomalous all-zero change rows; presence/absence logistic GLMs on all 632 plots and raw quartile/tercile contrasts as interpretable effect sizes. Best-supported scenario: recent (1993-2009) urbanization at the 1000 m landscape scale promoting the Unintentional pathway (interaction coef 3.55, 95% CI 0.60-6.50, p=0.018; count IRR 11.3, CI 1.33-95.3, p=0.026).

sub_hypo.text: Gardening-introduced species show no positive association between plot-level richness and urban cover at any examined scale.
sub_hypo.context: 632 plots in Barcelona province; urban cover examined for 1956, 1993 and 2009 within 50 m, 500 m and 1000 m buffers using controlled, dispersion-checked Poisson count models and BH-FDR correction.
sub_hypo.relations: No positive association between gardening-introduction richness and urban cover at any examined buffer scale.

sub_hypo.text: Agri-forest introductions show no detectable association between plot-level richness and urban cover.
sub_hypo.context: 632 plots in Barcelona province; urban cover examined for 1956, 1993 and 2009 within 50 m, 500 m and 1000 m buffers using controlled, dispersion-checked Poisson count models and BH-FDR correction.
sub_hypo.relations: No detectable association between agri-forest introduction richness and urban cover.

sub_hypo.text: Standing urban land-use level is a weak predictor of introduction-pathway-specific plant richness; the signal is associated with progressive urbanization rather than standing urban cover.
sub_hypo.context: 632 plots in Barcelona province; urban-level models for three years and three buffer scales compared with progressive/regressive change-category and urban-delta models for 1956–2009 and 1993–2009, with habitat, climate, distance and cropland controls.
sub_hypo.relations: Urban-cover levels have weak predictive associations with richness, whereas progressive urbanization, assessed through change categories and differences between urban-cover years, carries the signal, particularly for unintentionally introduced plants.

native_result.query: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promotes invasion of non-native plants in a pathway-specific way, operating mainly on occupancy (probability a plot is invaded) rather than local abundance: Gardening-introduced species show the strongest urban association (presence OR 5.37, p=0.002; 4.79 with habitat controls), Unintentional invaders require high urban intensity (OR 3.87, p<0.001) and are even more strongly promoted by cropland (OR 13.3, p<0.001), while AgriForest invaders are too rare for reliable estimates (OR 5.70, p=0.159, low power). Conditional on presence, urban cover does not raise invader counts (all count IRRs 0.8-1.1 n.s.), and species-level invasion success is driven by ecological versatility (habitat range IRR=1.88, p<0.001) rather than pathway or residence time (pathway x mrt LRT p=0.96), implying urbanization filters habitat-generalist species - especially ornamental origin ones - into urban and urbanizing landscapes.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded 3 tables (TSV parsing) + Newick tree (81 tips verified against phylo.tip.label). Descriptives: habitat x pathway table, temporal 4x3 chi-square (230.41, p=6.3e-47). Per-pathway hurdle GLMs (logistic presence + NB count|presence, HC1 robust SE) at 500m with urban_any/urban_hi bins + log1p cropland + elevation/rainfall/road/stream distances, with and without 9 habitat dummies; 1000m replication; 1956-2009 change-category models (5 anomalous rows excluded). Species-level NB with genus-clustered SEs after deduplicating 4 multi-pathway records. VIF and overdispersion diagnostics. Intercept-drop bug in initial draft detected via bivariate sign contradiction and corrected before final results.

native_result.query: What is the average length of original papers in Experimental Economics and that in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: Studies in Experimental Economics tend to have longer original papers compared to Psychology. The average length of original papers in Experimental Economics is 28 pages, whereas in Psychology, the average is 11 pages.
native_result.HypoB:
RESULT — Average length of original papers: Experimental Economics vs Psychology

FINAL ANSWER (natural-language, grounded in the data):
Original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than those in Psychology. In the dataset, the 18 Experimental Economics originals (project 'ee') average 28.0 pages (median 27.5, SD 7.4, range 16–45), whereas the 97 Psychology originals (project 'rpp') average only 11.2 pages (median 9, SD 6.3, range 1–31) — a gap of roughly 16.8 pages, i.e., economics originals are about 2.5× longer on average. The rpp mean is inflated relative to its median because of short-format articles: 42.3% of rpp papers are ≤7 pages and 55.7% are ≤10 pages (several are just 1–3 pages, reflecting short-report journal formats), which drags the mean down toward the short end while the median (9 pages) better represents the typical paper. Even so, the contrast is robust: by any measure (mean or median), Experimental Economics originals are far longer than Psychology originals in these replication projects.

SUPPORTING TABLE (unique-original level, one value per 'id'):

| Project                        | n (unique originals) | mean  | median | sd   | min | max |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|-------|--------|------|-----|-----|
| Experimental Economics (ee)    | 18                   | 28.00 | 27.5   | 7.37 | 16  | 45  |
| Psychology (rpp)               | 97                   | 11.22 | 9.0    | 6.30 | 1   | 31  |

Headline difference: 28.00 − 11.22 = 16.78 pages.

SENSITIVITY (U1) — Psychology bucket including Many Labs originals (ml1+ml3+rpp, 123 unique ids; 117 after title-dedup):
- Psychology incl. Many Labs: mean 11.07, median 9, SD 6.45, range 1–31 (title-dedup mean 11.16). Conclusion unchanged: ee ≈ 28 pages vs Psychology ≈ 11 pages regardless of whether Many Labs is included.

EXECUTION-VERIFIED CHECKS:
- A4 (drop flag): 7 rpp ids ARE flagged drop=True (rpp.154, rpp.46, rpp.59, rpp.69, rpp.73, rpp.77, rpp.82); 0 ee rows are dropped. Applying the flag would shrink the rpp sample from 97 to 90 originals and shift the rpp mean from 11.22 to 11.00 pages (median unchanged at 9). I retained all 97 in the primary result because 'drop' flags meta-analysis exclusions of O/R pairs (e.g., effect-estimation issues), not problems with the original papers themselves; the conclusion is insensitive either way.
- Duplicate handling: 'length' is constant within every 'id' (verified: 0 ids with >1 distinct length), and ee/rpp have exactly 1 row per id, so unique-original averaging equals all-rows averaging for the headline. For ml1/ml3 in the sensitivity bucket, I used the unique-id level (equivalently the aggregated=True rows).
- Data quality: length has no missing, zero, negative, or non-numeric values in ee or rpp; 1–3-page values (e.g., rpp.53 = 1, ml1.10 = 1) are genuine short-format articles and were retained.

WORKFLOW: pandas script analysis/average_paper_length.py — loads the study CSV (927 rows × 57 cols, 141 unique ids), verifies within-id constancy of length and the drop-flag status for rpp/ee, filters project ∈ {ee, rpp}, dedupes by 'id', computes mean/median/SD/min/max/n per project, and re-computes the Psychology bucket including ml1/ml3 (plus a title-dedup check) as the U1 sensitivity.

ASSUMPTIONS APPLIED: "Psychology" = project 'rpp' (with ml1/ml3 shown separately as sensitivity); average = arithmetic mean over unique originals; no outlier trimming; 'drop' flag not applied in the primary estimate (impact quantified: rpp mean 11.22 → 11.00 if applied).

LIMITATIONS: page counts are as recorded in the curated dataset and not externally validated; the rpp sample is dominated by 2008 short-format psychology articles, so the mean–median gap (11.2 vs 9) reflects journal format as much as discipline norms; the ee sample is small (n=18), so its mean carries more sampling uncertainty.

native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 respondents who were ever incarcerated (ever_jailed==1, n=289; jailed at some point 1985–1994), median 1985 wealth was extremely low overall (median $720; 45% at zero or negative net worth) and sharply stratified demographically. Racial hierarchy: white median $2,200 ≈ 7× the black median $320, while the hispanic median was $0 (white–hispanic gap effectively unbounded in ratio terms; 50% of hispanic ever-incarcerated at ≤$0). Gender gap: incarcerated men median $1,000 vs women $0 (70% of women vs 40% of men at ≤$0). Race×sex: white men $2,000 and white women $4,100 (n=12) at the top; black men $800 (0.40× white male) and hispanic men $700 (0.35×) in the middle; black and hispanic women at $0 (80–90% at ≤$0) at the bottom. Means greatly exceed medians in every group (e.g., white men mean $14,308 vs median $2,000), confirming right skew from a few high-wealth outliers. Context: the same race/sex gradient exists among the never-jailed at higher levels (white male $5,500; black male $1,500), so ever-incarcerated respondents were wealth-poor across all groups, with a black–white relative gap of similar magnitude inside and outside the incarcerated subsample. Timing caveat: the jailing flag spans 1985–1994 while wealth is 1985, so 1985 wealth may predate, coincide with, or postdate first jailing; this characterizes the eventually-incarcerated population's 1985 wealth, not a causal pre/post effect.

native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black NLSY79 respondents, ever having been jailed (1985-1994) is associated with sharply lower wealth by 1996 at every baseline (1985) wealth/income position, but the form of the association varies across the distribution: in the lowest baseline-wealth tercile (<= $0 in 1985; jailed n=76 vs never n=1,240) floor effects compress median differences (both $0), and the penalty appears as a much lower probability of accumulating any positive wealth by 1996 (22% vs 45%; mean gap -$17,181); in the middle tercile ($0-$3,830; n=39 vs 654), starting wealth is identical (median $1,400) yet jailed respondents' median wealth falls to $0 by 1996 vs $7,450 for never-jailed (mean gap -$29,393; DiD-style mean-change gap 1985->1996 of -$29,391); and in the highest tercile (>$3,830; n=44 vs 960), jailed respondents' median wealth does not grow at all, falling from $11,150 (1985) to $4,700 (1996) while never-jailed peers rise from $11,900 to $26,750 (median gap -$22,050; DiD mean-change gap -$59,008). The incarceration-wealth association among black individuals is therefore weakest in absolute wealth terms at the bottom (nothing-to-lose floor effect) and strongest in the middle and upper baseline-wealth strata, where it manifests as stagnant or negative wealth growth and a roughly halved probability of holding positive wealth. No income variable exists in the data, so 'income levels' are proxied by 1985 composite wealth terciles. These are observational associations conditional on baseline wealth, not causal estimates: jailing status spans 1985-1994 (the 1990 comparison is contemporaneous with the window, not a clean pre/post), composite wealth construction/units are undocumented, ~30-41% of wealth values are <=0 (floor effects), treated cells are small (39-76 per tercile), sex is the only covariate (jailed black respondents are overwhelmingly male: 143/1,465 men vs 16/1,548 women; the negative association holds in both sexes), and the processed file's complete absence of missing values precludes assessing panel attrition.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; verified race values white/black/'hipanic' [typo of hispanic, reported as observed], ever_jailed clean 0/1, zero missingness; wealth composites heavily right-skewed and zero-inflated with negative values, no top-coding). 2) Because the dataset has no income variable, proxied 'income levels' with baseline (1985) composite wealth, restricted to black respondents (n=3,013, 159 ever-jailed). 3) Stratified black respondents into 1985-wealth terciles (primary) and compared ever-jailed vs never-jailed within each stratum on 1990 and 1996 wealth levels (medians primary, means secondary, n per cell reported) and on within-stratum change 1985->1990 and 1985->1996 (DiD-style: jailed-group change minus never-jailed-group change); 1990 labeled contemporaneous-with-window, 1996 given equal weight as the post-window outcome. 4) Sensitivity: winsorization at 99th percentile, positive-wealth indicator, quartile stratification restricted to strata with jailed n>=30 (Q2 skipped, n=7). 5) Sex-stratified sanity check within the black subsample plus sex-demeaned pooled comparison. 6) Secondary white reference contrast with identical tercile design. Scripts: analysis/nls_incarceration_analysis.py, analysis/did_fix_and_quartiles.py; full printed output in analysis/analysis_output.txt.

native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality among white NLSY79 respondents fell on most relative-dispersion measures for both males and females, but the decline was driven by a swelling zero-wealth bottom rather than convergence of the upper tail. The zero-wealth share roughly doubled (white males 25.7%->43.3%; white females 20.3%->42.6%) and median wealth fell (males $15,601->$8,900; females $20,100->$8,825), while mean wealth and the 90th percentile rose (males: $88,163->$131,792 and $215k->$334k; females: $99,605->$128,837 and $243k->$332k). Relative dispersion among wealth holders narrowed for both sexes and slightly more for females: Gini on positive wealth males 0.688->0.623 (Δ=-0.066, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.090,-0.041]) vs females 0.681->0.599 (Δ=-0.082 [-0.107,-0.058]); CV males 2.78->2.41 vs females 2.66->2.33; p90/p10 among positives males 68.2->51.1 vs females 84.0->55.3. The full-distribution Gini including negatives barely moved (males 0.792->0.797; females 0.776->0.782; changes not significant by bootstrap), because the growing zero-wealth mass offsets the compression above zero, while p90/p50 rose sharply (both sexes ~+26-28, significant) as the median collapsed. Net characterization: wealth became more polarized (bimodal: zero bottom, richer top) while relative inequality among the positive-wealth population compressed for both sexes, with the female decline slightly stronger on dispersion measures and the male gains larger in mean/upper-tail dollars. Caveats: zeros may encode NLS missing codes rather than true zero wealth (though the doubling of zero share is itself a substantive finding and the exclude-zeros sensitivity preserves the inequality decline); the file has no person ID, so 1990 and 1996 are compared as repeated cross-sections; NLSY79 cohort attrition between waves cannot be assessed and could bias the comparison if wealth-selective.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows, 6 columns, no NaNs; white males n=3,469, white females n=3,630). For each sex x year (1990, 1996) computed mean, median, SD, CV, p10/p25/p50/p75/p90, quantile ratios (p90/p10 on positives, p90/p50, p75/p25), Gini via the O(n log n) sorted-rank formula on the full distribution (negatives included) and on positives only, top-10%/top-1% positive-wealth shares, and zero/negative/positive shares. Then computed within-sex 1990->1996 changes and the male-vs-female change-in-change, with 1,000-resample paired bootstrap 95% CIs (seed 20261019) for CV, Gini(all), Gini(pos), and p90/p50 changes. Sensitivity runs: (1) exact-duplicate removal (1,899 rows -> 10,114 unique); (2) deletion of the -$866,400 1990 outlier; (3) exclusion of zero-wealth respondents in either wave (n=6,152); (4) flooring negatives at zero. All sensitivity runs preserve the qualitative conclusions. Code: analysis.py; full printed results: analysis_output.txt.

Relative dispersion among wealth holders narrowed for both sexes and slightly more for females: Gini on positive wealth males 0.688->0.623 (Δ=-0.066, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.090,-0.041]) vs females 0.681->0.599 (Δ=-0.082 [-0.107,-0.058]); CV males 2.78->2.41 vs females 2.66->2.33; p90/p10 among positives males 68.2->51.1 vs females 84.0->55.3. The full-distribution Gini including negatives barely moved (males 0.792->0.797; females 0.776->0.782; changes not significant by bootstrap), because the growing zero-wealth mass offsets the compression above zero, while p90/p50 rose sharply (both sexes ~+26-28, significant) as the median collapsed. Net characterization: wealth became more polarized (bimodal: zero bottom, richer top) while relative inequality among the positive-wealth population compressed for both sexes, with the female decline slightly stronger on dispersion measures and the male gains larger in mean/upper-tail dollars. Caveats: zeros may encode NLS missing codes rather than true zero wealth (though the doubling of zero share is itself a substantive finding and the exclude-zeros sensitivity preserves the inequality decline); the file has no person ID, so 1990 and 1996 are compared as repeated cross-sections; NLSY79 cohort attrition between waves cannot be assessed and could bias the comparison if wealth-selective.

Because jail status spans 1985-1994, the significant 1985 gap indicates pre-incarceration selection, while the larger, baseline-adjusted gaps in 1990/1996 are consistent with an additional incarceration-associated wealth penalty.
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspected dataset (12,013 rows, no missingness; wealth composites right-skewed with zeros/negatives/extreme tails). Per year: Welch t-test, Mann-Whitney U, median test, bootstrap 95% CI of mean difference (5,000 resamples), Cliff's delta. Covariate-adjusted OLS with HC1 robust SEs (ever_jailed + race + sex); for 1990/1996 also controlled 1985 baseline wealth. Signed-log wealth sensitivity regressions. Holm correction across the three years for each test family. All conclusions robust across tests, adjustment sets, and correction.

native_result.query: How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of Socioeconomic Status and race on BA degree completion?
native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB: Academic characteristics (ASVAB achievement and class rank) account for a large share — roughly 30-60% — of the positive SES gradient in college attendance/completion proxied by dormitory residence, and essentially all of the small negative gradient for the Black-coded cohort (coefficient attenuates ~70-96% to ≈0); the Hispanic-coded cohort's positive gradient is not attenuated but amplified after academic controls. SES effects operate largely through measured academic ability. Because the file contains no direct BA-completion indicator, all statements concern attendance/completion proxied by ever living in a dorm/fraternity/sorority (NLSY79 residence code 3, any wave 1981-1996; sensitivity: 1985+ only).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61). Constructed outcomes: ever-dorm any wave 1981-96 (NLSY residence code 3) and sensitivity ever-dorm 1985+ waves. SES block: mother's grade, father's grade, ln(1+family income 1979), family size 1979. Race: cohort1/cohort2 indicators vs cohort3 reference. Covariates: sex, age. Academic block: four ASVAB scores re-standardized (raw values arrived on 165-825 scale despite 'Z Score' labels) + class-rank percentile (1 - rank/class size). Nested logistic regressions (statsmodels Logit): Model 1 SES+race baseline vs Model 2 + academic controls; complete-case primary (N=3,760), ASVAB-only (N=7,593), rank-only (N=4,041), and median-imputation + collapsed missing-indicator robustness (N=8,563). Reported log-odds, odds ratios, and % attenuation; % flagged unstable where |M1 log-odds|<0.05. Group means by racial/ethnic cohort reported for label sanity-checking. All 10 fits converged; post-1985 wealth/income excluded as post-treatment.

native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: The Black-vs-non-Black college-attendance gap in NLSY79 is SES-dependent in a widening pattern: near parity at low SES (3.4% vs 3.7%, −0.3 pp), small non-significant gap at middle SES (5.0% vs 6.5%, −1.5 pp), and a large significant gap at high SES (8.4% vs 19.3%, −11.0 pp; odds ratio ~0.35 vs ~0.87 at low SES; race×SES interaction p≈0.001). SES translates into college attendance far more steeply for non-Black than Black youths, so the Black disadvantage grows with socioeconomic status. This is measured with a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence proxy (1981-1996), not verified BA completion; commuter students are missed, undercounting may be race/SES-differential, data are observational, unweighted, and complete-case.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61); cleaned invalid grade=95 and identified income topcodes (75,001 in 1979). 2) Outcome: ever-dorm proxy (residence code 3 in any wave 1981-1996). 3) SES composite tertiles from standardized 1979 parental education (max of mom/dad) + 1979 family income (mean of available components). 4) Complete-case primary (N=12,532); race x SES tertile rates with Wilson CIs and rate differences. 5) Logistic regression ever_dorm ~ black x SES_tertile + age + sex (additive + multiplicative interaction); sensitivities: Black vs non-Black-non-Hispanic, parental-ed-only SES, income-only SES, income-missing indicator, ASVAB-adjusted (post-treatment caveat). Artifacts: analysis/nls_ba_analysis.py, analysis/rates_by_race_ses.csv, analysis/model_summary.txt.

sub_hypo.text: The Black-versus-non-Black college-attendance gap widens with socioeconomic status: near parity at low SES (3.4% versus 3.7%, −0.3 percentage points), a small non-significant gap at middle SES (5.0% versus 6.5%, −1.5 percentage points), and a large significant gap at high SES (8.4% versus 19.3%, −11.0 percentage points). SES translates into college attendance more steeply for non-Black than Black youths.

sub_hypo.relations: Race modifies the association between SES and ever having residence code 3 during 1981–1996. SES tertiles derive from the mean of available standardized components: maximum maternal/paternal education and 1979 family income. Attendance increases with SES in both racial groups, but more steeply among non-Black respondents, widening the Black disadvantage. Black-versus-non-Black odds ratios are approximately 0.87 at low SES and 0.35 at high SES; the race×SES interaction has p≈0.001. Logistic regression adjusts for age and sex, with additive and multiplicative interaction assessed.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The Black-vs-non-Black college-attendance gap in NLSY79 is SES-dependent in a widening pattern: near parity at low SES (3.4% vs 3.7%, −0.3 pp), small non-significant gap at middle SES (5.0% vs 6.5%, −1.5 pp), and a large significant gap at high SES (8.4% vs 19.3%, −11.0 pp; odds ratio ~0.35 vs ~0.87 at low SES; race×SES interaction p≈0.001). SES translates into college attendance far more steeply for non-Black than Black youths, so the Black disadvantage grows with socioeconomic status. This is measured with a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence proxy (1981-1996), not verified BA completion; commuter students are missed, undercounting may be race/SES-differential, data are observational, unweighted, and complete-case.

native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Median family net wealth of non-Black non-Hispanic ('white'-proxy) NLSY79 respondents exceeded that of Black and Hispanic respondents in every wealth wave from 1985 onward, and the disparity widened sharply: white/Black median ratio rose from 2.2x (1985: $3,500 vs $1,600) to 4.4x (1996: $42,600 vs $9,800), and white/Hispanic from 7.0x ($500) to 16.6x ($2,562); dollar gaps grew ~10-fold to $32,800 (Black) and $40,038 (Hispanic). The widening pattern is robust to a balanced-panel (all three waves) sensitivity and a positives-only median, and is not driven by negative/zero net worth or attrition direction. Caveats: cohort 3 is non-Black non-Hispanic, not strictly white; medians are unweighted sample medians (Black/Hispanic oversamples, no survey weights in file); 1996 missingness is high and differential (52.6% for cohort 3), though the balanced panel supports the conclusion; wealth is family/household-level; extreme wealth is top-coded (affects means, not medians).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 respondents, 61 vars). Verified racial/ethnic cohort (1=Black n=2002, 2=Hispanic n=3174, 3=non-Black non-Hispanic n=7510) and Sample ID codes mapping perfectly to cohorts (cross-sectional + poor-white oversample + military within cohort 3; Hispanic and Black oversamples otherwise). Primary analysis: unweighted available-case medians of Family net wealth for 1985/1990/1996 by cohort, with dollar gaps and white-referenced ratios; negatives/zeros kept. Sensitivities: balanced panel (n=5,739 observed in all waves) and positives-only medians. Supporting: asset-component medians among owners; attrition diagnostics (per-wave missingness, stayer/dropout 1985 medians); top-code checks. Outputs: analysis_nls_wealth.py, results_log.txt, nls_wealth_results.xlsx (5 sheets).

Supporting: asset-component medians among owners; attrition diagnostics (per-wave missingness, stayer/dropout 1985 medians); top-code checks. native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: In this NLS sample, the positive relation between socioeconomic status and the chance of completing a BA degree IS affected by racial lines: the SES gradient is significantly steeper for Black and (directionally) for Hispanic respondents than for White respondents (unadjusted interaction joint Wald p = 0.006), so racial disparities in BA completion are largest at low SES and nearly vanish at high SES (predicted BA probability at 1 SD below mean SES: White 2.9%, Black 0.6%, Hispanic 1.0%; at 1 SD above: 3.9%, 2.7%, 2.7%). However, the racial moderation is no longer detectable after controlling for ASVAB ability, class percentile, family size, and sex (joint p = 0.40), indicating the steeper minority SES gradient operates through, or is confounded with, measured academic ability and school performance rather than being a distinct race-specific SES effect. Given only 236 BA completions (~19 among Hispanic respondents), the Hispanic interaction is imprecise; the clear statistical contrast is Black vs White. The hypothesis is conditional on this sample and its unknown BA-completion measurement window.

native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: The Black advantage in BA-completion rates is most pronounced at the highest socioeconomic levels: raw rates show the Black-vs-non-Black gap turning positive only in the top SES decile (6.10% vs 4.78%, +1.3 pp), and after adjusting for ASVAB ability, class percentile, sex, and family size, the Black gap is positive above the median SES and largest and statistically significant around the 75th–95th SES percentiles. At low-to-mid SES Black respondents show a completion disadvantage (most negative gaps in deciles 2-3 and 7), which ability adjustment largely explains; the high-SES advantage persists beyond preparation. Findings are sensitive to binning (no positive gap bin at quartile resolution) and rest on rare events (~28 Black completers overall, ~5 in the top decile), so the top-level crossover itself is not individually significant (Fisher p=0.59); the support for the hypothesis is the monotonic SES gradient across bins, not any single cell.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, no missingness; SES continuous standardized, no documented bands). 2) Binned SES into pooled deciles (primary), quartiles and quintiles (sensitivity). 3) Computed raw BA-completion rates for Black, White, Hispanic, and pooled non-Black per bin with 95% normal-approx CIs on the difference and per-decile Fisher exact tests. 4) Fit logistic regressions: (a) BA ~ Black x (SES + SES^2) continuous interaction, unadjusted and adjusted for standardized ASVAB composite, class percentile, sex, family size — chosen after a pooled Black x decile-dummy model exhibited complete separation (zero Black events in the bottom decile); (b) Firth penalized logistic per decile for bias-reduced bin-level gaps. 5) Compared raw and adjusted gap gradients side by side and located where the Black advantage is largest/positive. Scripts: analysis_nls_ses.py, analysis_nls_ses_models.py, firth_check.py; tables in outputs/.

P0||G0.HypoB: The Black advantage in BA-completion rates is most pronounced at the highest socioeconomic levels: raw rates show the Black-vs-non-Black gap turning positive only in the top SES decile (6.10% vs 4.78%, +1.3 pp), and after adjusting for ASVAB ability, class percentile, sex, and family size, the Black gap is positive above the median SES and largest and statistically significant around the 75th–95th SES percentiles. At low-to-mid SES Black respondents show a completion disadvantage (most negative gaps in deciles 2-3 and 7), which ability adjustment largely explains; the high-SES advantage persists beyond preparation. Findings are sensitive to binning (no positive gap bin at quartile resolution) and rest on rare events (~28 Black completers overall, ~5 in the top decile), so the top-level crossover itself is not individually significant (Fisher p=0.59); the support for the hypothesis is the monotonic SES gradient across bins, not any single cell.
P0||G0.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, no missingness; SES continuous standardized, no documented bands). 2) Binned SES into pooled deciles (primary), quartiles and quintiles (sensitivity). 3) Computed raw BA-completion rates for Black, White, Hispanic, and pooled non-Black per bin with 95% normal-approx CIs on the difference and per-decile Fisher exact tests. 4) Fit logistic regressions: (a) BA ~ Black x (SES + SES^2) continuous interaction, unadjusted and adjusted for standardized ASVAB composite, class percentile, sex, family size — chosen after a pooled Black x decile-dummy model exhibited complete separation (zero Black events in the bottom decile); (b) Firth penalized logistic per decile for bias-reduced bin-level gaps. 5) Compared raw and adjusted gap gradients side by side and located where the Black advantage is largest/positive. Scripts: analysis_nls_ses.py, analysis_nls_ses_models.py, firth_check.py; tables in outputs/.

native_result.query: Between which two races is the factor of BA degree completion -0.9568 when compared to the other?
native_result.HypoA: There is a racial differential in BA degree completion rates between Black and White students with a factor of -0.9568.
native_result.HypoB: BA degree completion carries a factor of approximately -0.9568 in the comparison between Hispanic and White respondents: with White as the reference race, the Hispanic-vs-White logistic contrast is ≈ -0.92/-0.93 log-odds (OR ≈ 0.397, closest attainable to the reported -0.9568 / OR 0.384; residual ~0.03 log-odds disclosed), i.e., Hispanic respondents have substantially lower odds of completing a BA degree than White respondents (raw rates 1.44% vs 3.54%). Black respondents lie even further below White (coefficient ≈ -1.006, OR ≈ 0.366), confirming White as the advantaged group; only a post-hoc-tuned L2 penalty or a conditional interaction contrast could make Black-vs-White equal -0.9568 exactly.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection: 8,773×8, no missingness; BA 2.69% overall (White 3.54%, Hispanic 1.44%, Black 1.33%). 2) Main search: logistic regression of BA on race dummies × 32 covariate subsets (SES, ASVAB composite, PERCENTILE IN CLASS, SAMPLE_SEX, FAMILY SIZE) × 3 reference codings + race-only, all 6 ordered race-pair contrasts (~180 logit contrasts). 3) Scale checks: log-odds coefficient ≡ log(OR) matching, direct 2×2 cross-tab ORs, cloglog/probit/Poisson log-link variants. 4) Fallbacks: pairwise race-only logits, standardized vs raw ASVAB (invariance confirmed), per-sex fits. 5) Tie-break round: race×SEX and race×SES interaction models (conditional contrasts), percentile reversal (invariant), SES quartiles, 7 extreme-value subsamples, sklearn-style L2-penalized logit via verified Newton solver (C grid + bisection), and BA-as-predictor race-vs-race logits. 6) Decision rule: no specification within 1e-3 (or plain contrasts within 1e-2) of -0.9568; finalized best-supported pair Hispanic vs White (White reference) per protocol, residual disclosed, Black vs White as runner-up.

native_result.HypoA: Project leads (49.6%, 95% CI [49.219, 49.981]) and data scientists (61.389%, 95% CI [60.955, 61.822]) have the highest proportion of association with requirements in ML-enabled systems after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: In ML-enabled system projects, the two roles most strongly associated with requirements work are the Project Lead / Project Manager (51.031% of the 194 valid Q8 respondents; bootstrap 95% CI [43.814, 58.247]) and the Data Scientist (48.969%; 95% CI [42.268, 56.186]) — respondents most frequently indicated these two roles as the ones who address ML/requirements aspects in their organizations, well ahead of Business Analyst (25.773%), Developer (19.072%), Solution Architect (12.371%), Requirements Engineer (10.309%) and Tester (1.031%). Practically, ML requirements appear to be owned jointly by project leadership and data scientists rather than by dedicated requirements engineers. Note: these data-derived values and honest bootstrap CIs do not exactly match the externally supplied targets (49.6% [49.219, 49.981] and 61.389% [60.955, 61.822]); 61.389% (=221/360) and the ~0.38 pp CI widths are unattainable from n=194 via percentile bootstrap, so the reported values are the defensible data-grounded estimates, and the top-2 role identity (Project Lead/PM, Data Scientist) is robust across all sensitivity filters.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276 rows x 202 cols). Treated '-77' as question-skipped (82 respondents skipped the whole Q8 block and were excluded), '-99' as not-applicable free-text placeholder, and '0' as missing categorical. Operationalized 'association with requirements' via the Q8_ML_Addressing_* binary ('quoted'/'not quoted') role columns; denominators = the 194 respondents who answered Q8. Computed per-role proportions of 'quoted' for the seven fixed roles plus Other; ran a 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap (numpy default_rng seed 42) over valid Q8 respondents for 95% CIs; identified the two roles with the highest proportions. Sensitivity checks (point estimates): Status='Completed (31)' only, Completed + after-break, excluding D4_Role=='0', excluding 'Other, which one?', and both exclusions — all preserve the same top-2 ranking. Secondary operationalizations (Q1 importance of Problem Understanding & Requirements per role; Q12 difficulty of eliciting/analyzing requirements per role) were computed and rejected as primary because Q1 is role-generic (85.7–100% across roles) and Q12 measures difficulty rather than role association. Outputs: outputs/q8_primary_proportions_ci.csv, outputs/q8_sensitivity_proportions.csv; script: analysis_q8_roles.py.

GenH: BDD scenarios are the least-used named requirements documentation format in ML-enabled system projects, and ML Canvas is the second least-used. BDD scenarios are used by 4/194 respondents (2.06%, 95% bootstrap CI [0.52%, 4.12%]); ML Canvas is used by 15/194 (7.73%, 95% CI [4.12%, 11.86%]). Others ties ML Canvas but is not a named format., GenC: Requirements documentation in surveyed ML-enabled system projects; 194 valid Q10 respondents out of 276, excluding 82 question skips coded -77. Usage means 'quoted' rather than 'not quoted'; the 10 named formats are ranked, with Others and Not_Documented reported separately.

native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 cohort, individuals who show more impatient time preference — operationalized as putting less money into savings in 1989 — tend to have higher BMI: savers have about 0.3–0.4 lower BMI units than non-savers after covariate adjustment (adjusted β = −0.39, p = 0.001 for the saver indicator; put-in vs took-out contrast β = −0.35, p = 0.011), and greater net savings flow predicts significantly less BMI growth from 1981 to 1989 (adjusted β = −0.017 per log-dollar, p = 0.008; −0.19 BMI units per IQR). native_result.HypoB: Across the full sequence (4300-500 BCE), PC1 of the 12 capital-form Z variables is a general capital-accumulation axis (positive loadings on copper/gold, hoards, hatchets-swords, daggers, monument count/size, house size and pottery decoration; negative on pottery form, axes-celts, amber, sickle) that rises steadily from the Neolithic into the Bronze Age. Both the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and the Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE, data-table group SG; name mapping given by the task) sit on the negative, low end of this axis: MN starts relatively higher (PC1 about -0.6 at 3400 BCE) and drifts lower (about -1.8 by 3000 BCE), while the Younger Neolithic shows no trend, fluctuating around a low level with event-like spikes at 2700 BCE (monument count, Z=3.95) and 2300 BCE (daggers jumping from -0.58 to +0.80). Refitting the PCA on only the 12 MN+SG slices (sensitivity check; PC1 explains 43.4%) recasts PC1 as domestic/expressive capital (amber, pottery form and decoration, hoards, house size) versus prestige weapons and monument counts; on this axis the Middle Neolithic is consistently high and the Younger Neolithic drops sharply across the 2900-2800 BCE transition (about 3 SD) and stays low. 【最终自然语言假设 / Final natural-language hypothesis】

Between 3400 and 3000 BCE, the number of monuments and the abundance of axes/celts moved in close lockstep and followed a shared hump-shaped trajectory that was INVERSELY coupled to the trajectory of symbolic-capital elements. Both series started low at 3400 BCE (ZMonument = -0.46, ZBeil/AxesCelts = +0.37), rose to a pronounced joint peak at 3200 BCE (ZMonument = +0.91, ZBeil = +2.60), and fell back by 3000 BCE (ZMonument = -0.36, ZBeil = +0.80). Their synchrony is high at every time scale (annual interpolated series r = +0.93; the 5 century anchor observations r = +0.87; year-over-year changes r = +0.82), with the lead/lag profile peaking at lag 0 — monuments and axes rose and fell together, with no evidence that one led the other (the symmetric decay around lag 0 is largely an artifact of linear interpolation between century points).

Against the symbolic-capital elements the pattern is decoupled-to-inverse: hatchet/sword values stayed essentially flat (-0.43 to -0.42, giving only a weak descriptive positive co-movement with monuments, r ≈ +0.28, and near-zero with axes, r ≈ +0.03); dagger values were strictly constant (-0.58) throughout the window and therefore carry no within-window covariation; and house size — the only symbolic-capital element with substantial variance — declined steadily (z = +2.05 → +0.19, ≈ -0.45 z per century), co-varying negatively with monuments (levels r = -0.40; century-step changes r = -0.04, descriptive) and with axes (levels r = -0.26; century-step changes r = +0.50, descriptive, sign unstable across scales). Against the demographic background, pollen-based landscape openness (MEAN PC1) declined through the window (≈ -0.63 z/century) and shows weak negative level associations with monuments (r = -0.09) and axes (r = -0.19), while monument counts align positively with short-term phases of pollen increase (pollen growth rate r = +0.36, Spearman +0.41).

The 3200 BCE single-point peak must be read cautiously: only five century-spaced observations underlie the entire window, and the peak may be inflated by counting conventions or preservation bias.

BCE (z=1.54 plateau), and has fallen to ~0/negative by the total-peak centuries; MonumentCount has its absolute peak in the 27th c. BCE (z=3.95 raw mark; 2.58 interpolated century-mean) with a secondary peak coinciding with the total peak (z=1.71). BCE while amber had already declined out of the mix. gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: 园艺途径引入的非本土植物的流行程度随栖息地类型显著非均匀变化:在控制各栖息地非本土物种总丰度后,园艺来源记录的份额在湿地(0.56 [0.42–0.68])、海岸(0.53 [0.39–0.68])与针叶林(0.88 [0.53–0.98])显著高于城市参照(0.30;OR 2.97/2.71/16.5,p≤0.001),在农田显著最低(0.19;OR=0.54,p=0.005),河岸、草地、灌丛与城市无显著差异。假设:园艺引入种的相对优势沿'人为经营/水分富集梯度'分化——在人为营造或水分充足的生境中非本土植物群落以园艺来源为主,在农业景观中则以农业/林业与无意识引入为主;其机制背景是园艺物种入侵生态位宽度显著更窄(0.455 vs 0.720,p≈0.02,更依赖特定受管理生境),且园艺途径的区域引入份额由 Before-1500 的 0.17 升至 1985–2019 的 0.75,提供持续繁殖体压力。阔叶林(4/4)与岩石露头(0/1)因完全分离不可估,灌丛/草地样本过稀,均为方向性观察。

P1||G0.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
P1||G0.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
P1||G0.HypoB: 园艺途径引入的非本土植物的流行程度随栖息地类型显著非均匀变化:在控制各栖息地非本土物种总丰度后,园艺来源记录的份额在湿地(0.56 [0.42–0.68])、海岸(0.53 [0.39–0.68])与针叶林(0.88 [0.53–0.98])显著高于城市参照(0.30;OR 2.97/2.71/16.5,p≤0.001),在农田显著最低(0.19;OR=0.54,p=0.005),河岸、草地、灌丛与城市无显著差异。假设:园艺引入种的相对优势沿'人为经营/水分富集梯度'分化——在人为营造或水分充足的生境中非本土植物群落以园艺来源为主,在农业景观中则以农业/林业与无意识引入为主;其机制背景是园艺物种入侵生态位宽度显著更窄(0.455 vs 0.720,p≈0.02,更依赖特定受管理生境),且园艺途径的区域引入份额由 Before-1500 的 0.17 升至 1985–2019 的 0.75,提供持续繁殖体压力。阔叶林(4/4)与岩石露头(0/1)因完全分离不可估,灌丛/草地样本过稀,均为方向性观察。
P1||G0.WorkflowB: analysis.py executed (exit=0): data audit (count identity n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo==n.total verified in 632 rows; 81 tree tips bijection with phylo.tip.label); Eucalyptus zero niche-breadth issue resolved by discovering 25 zero-coded values -> dual reporting in auxiliary analysis only; duplicated cross-pathway rows handled with before(81 rows/42 gardening)/after(77/39) dual accounting; habitat-level gardening shares with Wilson + plot-level bootstrap CIs; main quasi-binomial GLM (ref=Urban, n=191 plots, scale=0.54, habitat F=7.26 p=5.5e-9); robustness via standard binomial (scale=1) and aggregated Poisson log-rate model (NB degenerate, alpha->0, replaced); Rock-outcrops sensitivity (p=2.1e-9); covariate sensitivity with VIF (habitat effect persists p=7.0e-10; elevation-temperature VIF 11-14 flagged); Moran's I residual check (I=0.007, p=0.15); auxiliary species-level contrasts and temporal pathway shares. Outputs: 10 CSV tables, 2 SVG figures, analysis log.

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: 在巴塞罗那省样地网络（632 样地，1956/1993/2009 景观快照）中，城市土地利用促进的是园艺渠道（Gardening，观赏/药用栽培引入）的非原生植物入侵：当样地处于城市化景观情境中——位于 Urban、Wetlands、Coastal、Riparian 等受扰动湿润生境且周边缓冲区（50–1000 m）含城市用地时，园艺入侵种显著富集（周边无城市覆盖时平均 0.03 种/样地，有覆盖时 0.37，随城市覆盖比例单调升至 0.58）；而园艺渠道入侵者入侵生态位幅度显著更窄（中位 0.36 vs 无意引入 0.87，p=0.0086），其成功依赖城市生境与园艺来源环境的匹配。对照反例：农田景观入侵以无意引入为主（83/108，77%），与城市生境渠道构成显著不同（χ²=6.29, p=0.043）。园艺渠道自 1985 年起占区域引入总量的 75%（χ²=230.4, p<1e-45）。此为数据支持的情境关联，非因果结论；生境校正后样地内连续城市覆盖的附加效应不显著（NB 系数 -0.71, p=0.12），效应主要体现在生境/景观层面。
native_result.WorkflowB: S0: TSV 解析(sep='\t')、计数一致性核验(632行全部 n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo=n.total)、种级按 Scientific_name 去重保留基础行剔除 4 个 '2' 后缀副本(81→77，系谱树含全部 81 tip 仅作校验)。S1 描述统计: 渠道时间趋势卡方、habitat×pathway 汇总、城市覆盖分位梯度、园艺份额与 Urban/Croplands 渠道构成卡方。S2 计数模型(N=632, 连续变量标准化、距离 log10、生境 8 组): Poisson(HC0) 预测变量搜索(urban.2009.1000m 最优 AIC 674.8)、n.gard 核心 Poisson+NB 模型(生境调整后城市覆盖系数 -0.69~-0.71, p≈0.12 不显著)、ZINB 尝试数值不稳(llf=nan)如实报告、urban×progressive 交互 +2.12 p=0.15 不稳定、对照渠道 n.unint/n.agfo 无城市覆盖响应。S3 种级机制(77 种): Kruskal-Wallis + Mann-Whitney，Gardening 生态位幅度显著窄于 Unintentional (p=0.0086)。S4: 整合为限定于数据支持范围的自然语言假设，含对照性反例与因果限度说明。

native_result.query: What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use is associated primarily with unintentionally introduced non-native plants (accidental introductions with trade, contaminated seed and tourism) and, secondarily, with gardening/ornamental introductions; agriculture-forestry introductions show no positive association with urban land use and were historically replaced by the other two pathways. Unintentional aliens in urbanized landscapes are ecological generalists (broader invaded niche breadth), consistent with urban environments filtering for versatile, human-associated species. The association partly operates through the urban habitat type itself, and causal attribution to urbanization remains hypothetical (cross-sectional design).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Input QC: 632-plot tab-separated plot dataset (37 cols, zero missing), 81-species trait dataset, 12-cell temporal contingency table, 81-tip Newick tree (76/81 tip labels matched). 2) Main analysis (A): per-pathway hurdle models (logit presence + Poisson count on positives) on 632 plots with urban land-cover share (2009, 500 m buffer) as focal covariate; covariates: log elevation, 10-level habitat, log road/stream distance, annual temperature and rainfall, b-splines of UTM x/y; weak-ridge IRLS to handle complete separation in zero-positive habitat levels; joint bootstrap (1000) for pathway contrasts and CIs; sensitivity across 50/500/1000 m buffers x 1956/1993/2009; partial-adjustment models to diagnose habitat-mediated attenuation. 3) Auxiliary (B): Kruskal-Wallis comparisons of invasion-success metrics (invaded plots, occupancy, niche breadths, residence time, height) across pathways. 4) Temporal corroboration (C): pathway counts/shares per introduction period, chi-square test. Phylogenetic analysis skipped (no tree libraries available; 5 duplicate-species tip labels missing) - noted as limitation.

P1||G0.HypoB: 城市土地利用是按引入途径区分的过滤器而非无差别放大器，其作用集中于景观尺度（500–1000m）而非 50m 微生境：园艺途径主导当代种库（份额 17%→75%）但对当前城市覆盖不敏感；无意引入种（入侵生态位最宽）随周边城市覆盖增加（1000m 交互 β=+0.73, IRR≈2.1）；农业林业引入种随城市化被强烈排除（IRR 低至 0.09，p=0.014）；1956–2009 历史土地利用变化在控制当前覆盖后无独立效应（p>0.7，AIC 支持当前覆盖模型）。
P1||G0.WorkflowB: 清洗与聚合（4 条 duplicated 记录按学名聚合为 77 物种；632 样方转长格式 1896 行，plot_id 聚类稳健 SE）→ A: 4×3 列联表卡方+份额趋势 → B: Kruskal-Wallis + NB GLM + PGLS 敏感性（λ̂≈0，与普通模型一致）→ C: 三尺度 NB GLM（count ~ pathway×urban.2009 + 生境/气候/距离协变量），交互 2-df LRT，与历史变化模型按 AIC 分别比较，辅以 offset 组成模型、VIF 诊断与边际预测效应量

Question: For both HypoA and HypoB, what are the different variables found in the hypotheses?         Return your answer as a JSON object in the following format:
        ```json
        {{
        "sizeA": num of variables used in HypoA
        "sizeB": num of variables used in HypoB
        "intersection": num of variables common in HypoA and HypoB. Use *fuzzy matching* to determine intersection, accounting for paraphrases or slightly different surface forms
        "explanation": a short text explanation about the variables
        }}```
        Answer:

score.explanation: HypoA uses urban land cover, plant invasion abundance, and introduction pathway (gardening versus unintentional). HypoB shares these three variables and additionally mentions spatial buffer scale (50–1000 m), introduction period, pathway-specific introduction share, invaded niche breadth, and historical land-use change. Agriculture/forestry is another category of introduction pathway, not a separate variable. Coefficients, IRRs, p-values, and AIC are statistical summaries rather than additional variables.

rel.question:
Question: Does HypoB exhibit the same relation as HypoA?
        Compare using following example hierarchy of relationships (based on specificity):         "there exists a relationship" > "positive relationship" > "positive AND (linear OR quadratic)" > "positive AND linear".
        Options: A) very similar B) similar but general than HypoA C) different
        Return your answer as a JSON object in the following format:
        ```json
        {{
        "answer": one of the options from A) very similar B) similar but general than HypoA C) different
        "explanation": a short text explanation about the relationship comparison
        }}```
        Answer:
rel.answer: {"answer":"C) different","explanation":"HypoA asserts that urban land use reduces invasion by gardening plants relative to unintentionally introduced plants. HypoB instead asserts no sensitivity of gardening plants to current urban cover, a positive effect on unintentional introductions, and a strong negative effect on agriculture/forestry introductions. Thus, although the relative contrast is compatible, HypoB specifies different pathway-specific relationships rather than the same reduction."}

native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality among white males and white females underwent polarization: overall within-group inequality (Gini) stayed essentially unchanged (male 0.792→0.798, female 0.776→0.782, changes not significant at 95%), but the distribution polarized — the bottom collapsed (median fell 43% for males from $15,601 to $8,900 and 56% for females from $20,100 to $8,825 in nominal terms; zero-wealth share nearly doubled from 25.7%→43.3% for males and 20.3%→42.6% for females) while the upper tail stretched (P90/P50 rose from 13.8→37.5 for males and 12.1→37.6 for females). Meanwhile the between-sex gap reversed: in 1990 white females had higher median and mean wealth than white males (median gap male−female = −$4,499; mean gap = −$11,442), but by 1996 this female advantage disappeared (median gap +$75; mean gap +$2,956). Robustness: excluding |wealth|>$3M and winsorizing at 1%/99% leave all directional conclusions unchanged; excluding zeros raises 1996 medians and lowers the Gini (0.64 male, 0.62 female), indicating the observed pattern is driven by households sliding into zero wealth — if the 38% 1996 zero share partly reflects missing values coded as zero, the median decline is overstated but the disappearance of the female wealth advantage holds under both treatments. All values are nominal (no inflation adjustment).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded 12,013-row NLSY79-derived dataset (no missing values); subset white respondents (male n=3,469, female n=3,630); computed for 1990 and 1996 composite wealth: mean, median, percentiles (P1/P25/P50/P75/P90/P99), P90/P50, mean/median ratio, Gini coefficient (with and without negative truncation), zero/negative shares, and top-10%/top-1% wealth shares; computed between-sex gaps (male−female); ran sensitivity analyses (drop |wealth|>$3M, winsorize 1%/99%, drop zeros, truncate negatives); assessed significance of Gini changes via 1,000-replicate bootstrap CIs. Outputs: wealth_inequality_results.csv, between_sex_gaps.csv, analysis scripts.

sub_hypo.text: Between 1990 and 1996, within-sex wealth inequality among white respondents remained essentially unchanged: male Gini increased from 0.792 to 0.798 and female Gini from 0.776 to 0.782, with neither change significant at the 95% level.
sub_hypo.context: White respondents in the NLSY79-derived dataset, analyzed separately for males (n=3,469) and females (n=3,630), using nominal composite wealth in 1990 and 1996; significance assessed using 1,000-replicate bootstrap confidence intervals.
sub_hypo.relations: Within-sex Gini coefficients remained essentially stable from 1990 to 1996 despite small, statistically nonsignificant increases.

sub_hypo.text: Between 1990 and 1996, white males' and white females' wealth distributions polarized: medians declined and zero-wealth shares nearly doubled, while upper-tail wealth increased relative to median wealth.
sub_hypo.context: White male and female respondents in the NLSY79-derived dataset; 1990 and 1996 composite wealth measured in nominal dollars without inflation adjustment.
sub_hypo.relations: Male median wealth fell 43%, from $15,601 to $8,900, and female median wealth fell 56%, from $20,100 to $8,825. Zero-wealth shares increased from 25.7% to 43.3% for males and from 20.3% to 42.6% for females. P90/P50 increased from 13.8 to 37.5 for males and from 12.1 to 37.6 for females.

sub_hypo.text: The female wealth advantage among white respondents disappeared between 1990 and 1996, with both median and mean male-minus-female wealth gaps reversing sign.
sub_hypo.context: Between-sex comparisons among white respondents in the NLSY79-derived dataset, using nominal composite wealth in 1990 and 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Females had higher median and mean wealth in 1990: male-minus-female gaps were −$4,499 and −$11,442, respectively. By 1996 these gaps reversed to +$75 and +$2,956.

sub_hypo.text: Excluding observations with absolute wealth above $3 million or winsorizing wealth at the 1st and 99th percentiles leaves all directional conclusions about white respondents' wealth changes unchanged.
sub_hypo.context: Sensitivity analyses of nominal 1990 and 1996 composite wealth among white male and female respondents in the NLSY79-derived dataset.
sub_hypo.relations: The directions of median declines, increasing zero-wealth shares and upper-tail-to-median ratios, and reversal of the female wealth advantage persist under exclusion of |wealth| > $3 million and 1%/99% winsorization.

sub_hypo.text: Excluding zero wealth raises 1996 medians and lowers Gini coefficients among white respondents, indicating that the observed pattern is driven by households sliding into zero wealth. If the reported 38% 1996 zero share partly reflects missing values coded as zero, the median decline is overstated, but the disappearance of the female wealth advantage holds whether zeros are retained or excluded.
sub_hypo.context: Zero-exclusion sensitivity analysis of white male and female respondents' nominal 1990 and 1996 composite wealth in the NLSY79-derived dataset; missing values coded as zero are a conditional possibility, not an established finding.
sub_hypo.relations: Dropping zeros increases 1996 median wealth and reduces 1996 Gini to 0.64 for males and 0.62 for females. Potential missing-as-zero coding would overstate the median decline, while the disappearance of the female wealth advantage is robust to retaining versus excluding zeros.

native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 cohort data, individuals jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed=1) had significantly lower composite wealth than never-jailed individuals in all three measured years (1985, 1990, 1996; all p < 1.6e-10 across Welch t, log1p-transformed Welch t, and Mann-Whitney U tests, robust to removing 1,899 duplicate rows). The largest and most question-relevant gaps occur post-incarceration in 1990 and 1996, where the jailed group's median wealth was $0 versus $10,500 and $8,500 for the never-jailed (mean gaps of $57,598 and $85,063, i.e., jailed-group means only ~22% and ~19% of the comparison group). The 1985 gap (median $720 vs $3,600) was measured before/within the incarceration window and is therefore better interpreted as pre-existing socioeconomic disadvantage (selection) rather than a consequence of incarceration. Hypothesis (correlational, not causal): having a criminal record is associated with substantially and significantly lower wealth in the post-incarceration years 1990 and 1996 — and this pattern holds across race and sex subgroups — while the 1985 deficit reflects prior disadvantage. The dataset cannot support a causal claim because confounders such as education and earnings history are unavailable.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows x 6 cols, zero missingness). 2) Main analysis: compared ever_jailed=1 (n=289) vs ever_jailed=0 (n=11,724) on composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996 using (a) Welch t-test on raw values, (b) Welch t-test on log1p-transformed values, (c) two-sided Mann-Whitney U; reported group means, medians, SDs, mean and median differences. 3) Duplicate-row sensitivity: dropped 1,899 exact duplicates (n=10,114; jailed n=239) and reran all tests; conclusions identical across all years and tests. 4) Stratified analyses by race (white n1=69, black n1=159, hipanic n1=61) and sex (male n1=252, female n1=37), with small subgroups treated descriptively. 5) Aggregated per-year significance and formulated the natural-language hypothesis with interpretation boundary for the 1985 baseline (pre/within incarceration window). Outputs: outputs/main_results.csv, outputs/dedup_sensitivity_results.csv, outputs/analysis_output.txt.

native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB: 在 NLSY79 中，家庭社会经济地位与种族对'截至 1979 年的大学入学轨迹'（BA 完成的结构性代理：1979 年最高受教育年限≥13）的影响呈不对称调整模式：加入学业特征（ASVAB 标准化成绩均值与高中班级排名百分位）后，SES 的标准化系数被吸收约 50–60%（0.84→0.37，完整案例、同样本对照与多重插补一致），表明 SES 与教育获得的关联大部分经由学业表现传导；但种族效应未被解释反而增强——条件于 ASVAB 后，Black（OR 1.43→2.45）与 Hispanic（由不显著升至 OR≈3.9）青年在同等分数下进入大学轨道的概率显著更高。学业特征主要解释阶层差异而非种族差异；班级排名对 SES 效应几乎无额外吸收（额外缩减 <3%），ASVAB 是主要通道。结论严格限定于早期教育获得（数据无毕业后学位记录），'吸收'按统计分解而非严格因果中介理解。

native_result.HypoB: With education right-censored at 1979, as-of-1979 BA completion (highest grade >=16) is too rare (32/8,870) to show any Black advantage at any SES level: Black vs non-Black/non-Hispanic rates are 0.10% vs 0.12% (Low SES), 0.65% vs 0.25% (Mid), 0.29% vs 0.63% (High), and race x SES-tertile interactions are non-significant (p = 0.42/0.71; MI-pooled p = 0.40/0.74). Family-of-origin SES strongly raises attainment at a similar rate for both groups (High-vs-Low log-odds +1.66 for BA, +1.03 for any postsecondary, both significant). The only supported Black advantage appears in the secondary outcome (any postsecondary, >=13): conditional on age and ASVAB achievement, Black respondents show higher postsecondary exposure (+1.08 log-odds, p<0.001), an advantage largest at Low/Mid SES and significantly attenuated at High SES (interaction -0.76, p=0.014); unadjusted, Black postsecondary exposure is lower at every SES level with the widest deficit at High SES (-6.4 pp). Hypothesis: the Black-non-Black difference in college attainment in these data does not depend on SES level — SES is a common, race-similar escalator — and any Black advantage is detectable only after adjustment for age and achievement, concentrated at lower-to-middle SES.
