native_result.query: Which technique is considered the most commonly used by respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 69.399% indicating so (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: Interviews (69.399% respondents saying so, 95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) are the most commonly used technique considered by the respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: Interviews are the elicitation technique most commonly used by respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: 97 of 194 answering respondents (50.0%, 95% percentile-bootstrap CI [42.784%, 57.216%], 10,000 resamples) indicated using interviews, the highest proportion among the five named Q9 techniques (Scenarios 38.66%, Prototyping 38.66%, Workshops and meetings 38.14%, Observation 32.99%). The ranking is robust to denominator choice (35.145% of all 276 rows with '-77' as non-use; 55.747% among respondents quoting at least one technique). Note: the quoted 69.399% (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) could not be regenerated from this transformed file (Likert levels collapsed to quoted/not-quoted; maximum reproducible proportion 50.0%; CI half-width implies effective n ≈ 72,000, inconsistent with n ≈ 194) and is reported as an unresolvable discrepancy.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276 respondents, 202 columns). Identified Q9_ML_Elicitation_{Interviews, Scenarios, Prototyping, Workshops_Meetings, Observation, Others(+Free)} as the candidate elicitation items. Verified sentinels: '-77' marks unanswered Q9 items (identically the same 82 rows, all Status 'Suspended (22)' — survey dropouts) and was excluded; '-99'/'-66' are NA sentinels in free-text/numeric columns; free-text Others excluded from ranking. Computed quoted-proportions per technique under three labeled denominators (n=194 primary; n=276 robustness; n=174 quoters). Ran 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap (numpy default_rng, seed 20240613) over the 194 valid respondents for 95% CIs. Verified Interviews strictly highest point estimate. Attempted reconciliation with the quoted 69.399% figure and CI [69.062, 69.735]: no natural statistic in the file matches (exact fraction 127/183 = 69.399% has no corresponding count of 127; CI half-width implies n ≈ 72,049), reported as an uncertainty. Saved point estimates and bootstrap CIs to CSV.

native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Over 1975-2015, Sub-Saharan Africa persistently devoted a larger share of GNI to education than developing countries (LMC) - mean 4.30% vs 3.50% of GNI, converging to near parity by 2015 (3.15% vs 3.06%) - yet SSA's GNI per capita remained lower and grew more slowly in the only fully observed income window (2011-2015 CAGR 1.25% vs 3.29%). In this aggregate panel, education expenditure (% of GNI) shows no positive association with per-capita income in either group in raw levels, and the association is weaker (less negative, turning mildly positive) in Sub-Saharan Africa than in LMC once the common time trend is removed (SSA slope +0.033 vs LMC -0.200 log-points per pp of GNI; interaction delta=-0.23, HAC se 0.05). Hypothesis: the marginal payoff to education-expenditure shares is smaller in Sub-Saharan Africa than in developing countries - SSA's higher and earlier investment share did not translate into a detectable income advantage. Because SSA income is observed in only 5 of 41 years and all series are group aggregates, this comparison is suggestive and descriptive, not causal or precisely identified.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected and reshaped the wide 12x45 WDI file (2 groups x 6 series, 1975-2015) to a long group-year panel (artifacts/long_panel.csv). 2) Pooled two-group OLS with HAC(1) SEs: ln(GNI) ~ edu + LMC + edu:LMC, on all 46 available income observations and on the strict 2011-2015 overlap (n=10), reporting group-specific slopes (SSA beta, LMC beta+delta) and the interaction delta with delta-method SEs. 3) Within-group diagnostics: SSA-only OLS 2011-2015 (n=5); LMC-only 1975-2015 (n=41) with and without a linear year trend; pooled model with year trend as robustness. 4) Descriptive 1975-2015 comparison of expenditure shares, enrollment ratios, correlations, and 2011-2015 income growth. 5) No imputation; complete-case throughout; documentation mismatches (GDP 2010 US$ vs GNI 2015 US$; % of total expenditure vs % of GNI; SSF vs SSA code) flagged and resolved in favor of the data.

native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In NLSY79, individuals who put more money into savings in 1989 (net savers, a proxy for higher time preference/patience) have consistently lower BMI in 1989 and 1992: adjusted for demographics, cognition and family background the gap is ~0.6–1.0 BMI units (p<1e-5), and adjusting further for 1981 baseline BMI it is ~0.30 units (p=0.005), with obesity odds ~31% lower (OR 0.69). native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: The Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and the Diversity in Pottery Decoration simultaneously increases in the 18th century BCE — the century labeled 1700 BCE (1800–1701 BCE convention). In that single century the PotteryForm z-score plunges from +0.74 to −1.13 (Δ = −1.87, z = −3.38, the largest one-century decline in the entire 4100–500 BCE record) while PotteryDecoration jumps in the same century from −0.48 to +0.97 (Δ = +1.45, z = +3.18), then continues to its maximum plateau of +1.53 by 1000 BCE, while Form remains locked at its series minimum of −1.13 through 500 BCE. 1700 BCE is the only century in the record where a strong Form decline (z ≤ −1) coincides with a strong Decoration rise (z ≥ +1); the only other Form-decline century (2800 BCE) shows Decoration falling as well.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded time_series_data.csv (3,601 annual rows, CE −4100..−500, CE negative = BCE) and extracted the century-mark z-series for PotteryForm/PotteryDecoration (raw columns hold exactly 37 values at the 100-year marks CE −4100..−500; the annual _inter columns are linear interpolations verified numerically identical at the century marks). 2) Computed one-century changes and z-scored them across the series. 3) Defined collapse = Form decline event (z-scored change ≤ −1) and increase = Decoration rise event (z-scored change ≥ +1); a purely level-based collapse flag was rejected because it mislabels the post-collapse plateau (1600–500 BCE, Form constant at −1.13) as collapse. 4) Required coincidence of both events within the same century bin → unique century: 1700 BCE. 5) Cross-checked against (a) the annual PotteryForm_inter/PotteryDecoration_inter series (the step falls entirely within the 1700 BCE century) and (b) capital.csv ZKeform/Zkeverz (BCE labels verified to align with time_series_data CE = −BCE; BCE 1700 row identical). Data-quality flags: capital.csv rows BCE 4300/4200 duplicate the CE −500 values and lie outside the time-series range (excluded, non-driving); the pollen openness record (CE −4785..−702, Belau/Woserin PC1 with interpolated and 50–250-year smoothed variants) fully covers the pottery window and is treated as supporting context only.

Landscape openness collapsed to its period minimum around 1500 BCE and then rebounded at the fastest rates of the entire window through 1400-1300 BCE, reaching maximum openness levels around 1300-1200 BCE. This pollen-based growth phase coincides with the broadest rise in capital indicators (symbolic weapons, social house/monument investment, and economic metals/depots all jump into 1400-1301 BCE), although pottery-related (cultural) indicators remain flat - a noted exception - and the latest economic uptick (depot hoards at 1100 BCE) postdates the pollen-growth peak.

## PC1 strength & stability

**Middle Neolithic 3400–3000 BCE (5 slices, group MN):**
3400: −0.59 | 3300: −1.30 | 3200: −1.78 | 3100: −1.49 | 3000: −1.81

YN mean is slightly less negative than MN mean, and its end value (−0.42) is the highest Neolithic-century score — a first step toward the positive Bronze-Age regime.

## Pollen-openness overlay (Belau+Woserin MEAN; SMOOTH_MEAN_100y similar)
MN 3400–3000: +0.08 → +0.54 → −1.02 → −1.09 → −1.86 — openness rises to ~3300 then falls steeply to the period minimum at 3000.

## Draft data-grounded hypothesis (for your review, not final)
The first principal component — which contrasts metal prestige goods, hoards/depots and pottery decoration (positive) against amber, utilitarian axes and pottery-form emphasis (negative) — characterizes both Neolithic phases as firmly on the negative, "pre-metal-wealth" side of the forms-of-capital gradient, but the two phases differ in trajectory. The Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE) begins at its period maximum (PC1 −0.59 at 3400, with large houses, copper/gold and pottery-form emphasis) and declines steadily to −1.81 by 3000 BCE as monumental activity briefly peaks (3200) and then house size and metal presence collapse — a phase of decreasing capital concentration. The Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE) starts near this low and recovers irregularly to −0.42 by 2300 BCE, punctuated by a monumental-construction peak around 2700 BCE and a daggers/metal uptick at 2300 BCE — i.e., a phase of fluctuating but net-increasing capital diversification that preludes the positive, metal-dominated Bronze-Age regime. Both phases track landscape openness: openness and PC1 fall together through the MN (r ≈ 0.72) and fluctuate together in the YN (r ≈ 0.51), suggesting that periods of more open (agriculturally expanded) landscape coincided with higher scores on the wealth/hoarding dimension of capital.

## Caveats / instability flags
1. PC1 explains only 30.3% of variance (PC2 19.5%) — the two-dimensional structure matters; conclusions rest on the leading tendency only.
2. Within-window constant/near-constant variables (ZDolch, ZSichel in MN; ZDolch, ZCU_AU until 2300) contribute no within-period signal; period-internal trends are driven by a few variables (MN: Zhausgr, ZCU_AU, ZMW; YN: ZMonument, Zamber, Zkeverz).
3. YN trajectory is non-monotonic; the "rising" characterization depends on endpoint comparison (2900 → 2300), not a steady trend.
4. Small n (5 and 7 slices); correlation values are descriptive.
5. Pollen series are interpolated/smoothed products, not independent annual observations.

This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
P0||G0.HypoB: The symbolic-capital components split across the two leading PCs: on PC1 (30.3% variance) hatchets/swords (+0.30), daggers (+0.27) and house size (+0.23) all load moderately positive together with the prestige goods copper/gold (+0.41), pottery decoration (+0.38) and depots (+0.34), and against subsistence/utility items (sickles, axes/celts, pottery form, amber), so on the dominant wealth-accumulation axis the symbolic trio is not separated from economic capital; on PC2 (19.5% variance) the trio is heterogeneous — house size (+0.33) is displaced onto the second axis with axes/celts (+0.47), amber (+0.44), monument size (+0.39) and monument count (+0.29), while daggers (+0.07) and hatchets/swords (+0.05) are near zero, remaining defined almost entirely by PC1. Weapons are thus pure indicators of the overall capital gradient, whereas house size additionally tracks an independent settlement/monumentality dimension.
P0||G0.WorkflowB: Parsed capital.csv with decimal commas, dropped group/color, 12 Z columns as variables over 39 100-year BCE slices (4300–500); standardized columns and ran correlation-matrix PCA (SVD). Repeated on deduplicated unique period rows (37). Robustness: time_series_data.csv *_inter columns averaged into the same 100-year BCE bins (37 slices) and re-run. Reported eigenvalues, variance shares, PC1–PC3 loadings, communalities, score–time correlations, and PC1/PC2 loading correlations between runs. PC1 sign fixed only for reporting (majority-positive sum); signs are arbitrary.

Landscape openness from pollen (Belau/Woserin) declines in step with the symbolic-capital index (r = +0.88) — context only, not a causal claim.

native_result.HypoA: In 1700 BCE, for the first time, Diversity in Pottery Decoration shows a significant increase while Diversity in Pottery Form experiences a notable decline. This marks a unique divergence in the growth trends of these two cultural capital variables.
native_result.HypoB: Diversity in Pottery Decoration and Diversity in Pottery Form first show opposite growth trends in the 18th century BCE, around 1700 BCE: Pottery Decoration diversity rises sharply (z-score -0.48 to +0.97, delta = +1.45, about 3.4 SD of its historical century-to-century variability) while Pottery Form diversity drops simultaneously to its lowest recorded level (+0.74 to -1.13, delta = -1.87). This is the only century in the entire 4300-500 BCE record where Decoration increases and Form declines simultaneously, coinciding with the Late Neolithic-to-Bronze-Age (LN to OBA) cultural transition. Archaeologically, this marks a reorganization of ceramic production: vessel forms became standardized (form diversity collapsing to a plateau of -1.13 lasting to 500 BCE) while decorative diversity was elaborated to its maximum (+0.97 to +1.53), i.e., a divergent style strategy in which standardized shapes were differentiated through surface ornamentation.

native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway shows strongly habitat-dependent prevalence: its per-plot incidence is highest in low-elevation, wet/mesic and human-influenced habitats (Wetlands 50%, Urban 48%, Coastal 45%, Riparian 36% of plots) and near-zero in natural upland/mature habitats (Meadows 8%, Coniferous forests 6.5%, Broad-leaved forests 4.4%, Scrublands 1.9%, Rock outcrops 0%); as a share of introductions, gardening dominates in wetlands and coastal plots (~54–56%) and in the few introductions recorded in forests (~88–100%, small n), while urban and cropland pools are unintentional-dominated (69–77%) despite widespread gardening presence. The pattern is highly significant (χ²=139.4, p≈1e-25; permutation p=1e-5; Poisson GLM LR p≈2e-37) and persists after adjusting for elevation and surrounding urban/cropland cover, with elevation the strongest single gradient — consistent with gardening introductions spreading from nearby ornamental plantings into accessible lowland mesic habitats, mirroring the temporal rise of gardening from 17% (before 1500) to 75% (1985–2019) of introductions.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded 4 files (2 tab-separated with quoted headers); verified count identity n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo=n.total in 632/632 plots and 81/81 phylo.tip.label↔tree leaf matches; built habitat×pathway table with Wilson CIs; tested among-habitat gardening incidence (χ², B=100k permutation, Poisson & negative-binomial GLMs); fitted covariate logit models (elevation, urban/cropland 50m/500m, 1956–2009 change indices) with and without habitat; temporal-share enrichment from the contingency table; species-level cross-check; phylogenetic tree explicitly declared unused (no plot↔species join).

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The gardening pathway shows strongly habitat-dependent prevalence: its per-plot incidence is highest in low-elevation, wet/mesic and human-influenced habitats (Wetlands 50%, Urban 48%, Coastal 45%, Riparian 36% of plots) and near-zero in natural upland/mature habitats (Meadows 8%, Coniferous forests 6.5%, Broad-leaved forests 4.4%, Scrublands 1.9%, Rock outcrops 0%); as a share of introductions, gardening dominates in wetlands and coastal plots (~54–56%) and in the few introductions recorded in forests (~88–100%, small n), while urban and cropland pools are unintentional-dominated (69–77%) despite widespread gardening presence. The pattern is highly significant (χ²=139.4, p≈1e-25; permutation p=1e-5; Poisson GLM LR p≈2e-37) and persists after adjusting for elevation and surrounding urban/cropland cover, with elevation the strongest single gradient — consistent with gardening introductions spreading from nearby ornamental plantings into accessible lowland mesic habitats, mirroring the temporal rise of gardening from 17% (before 1500) to 75% (1985–2019) of introductions.

P0||G0.query: In what context does the gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants show different prevalence styles across habitat types?
P0||G0.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
P0||G0.HypoB: The gardening pathway shows strongly habitat-dependent prevalence: its per-plot incidence is highest in low-elevation, wet/mesic and human-influenced habitats (Wetlands 50%, Urban 48%, Coastal 45%, Riparian 36% of plots) and near-zero in natural upland/mature habitats (Meadows 8%, Coniferous forests 6.5%, Broad-leaved forests 4.4%, Scrublands 1.9%, Rock outcrops 0%); as a share of introductions, gardening dominates in wetlands and coastal plots (~54–56%) and in the few introductions recorded in forests (~88–100%, small n), while urban and cropland pools are unintentional-dominated (69–77%) despite widespread gardening presence. The pattern is highly significant (χ²=139.4, p≈1e-25; permutation p=1e-5; Poisson GLM LR p≈2e-37) and persists after adjusting for elevation and surrounding urban/cropland cover, with elevation the strongest single gradient — consistent with gardening introductions spreading from nearby ornamental plantings into accessible lowland mesic habitats, mirroring the temporal rise of gardening from 17% (before 1500) to 75% (1985–2019) of introductions.

native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted the invasion of ornamental, Gardening-pathway plants specifically in peri-urban landscapes that were progressively urbanized between 1956 and 2009 (plots where ≥50% of the surrounding 50-m buffer shifted to urban/cropland cover): such plots hold ~55% Gardening-introduced non-native records vs ~34% in unchanged and ~30% in regressive landscapes, with garden escapes (tall perennial shrubs/trees like Robinia pseudoacacia, Phytolacca americana, Araujia sericifera, reproducing vegetatively, narrow invaded niche breadth median 0.36 vs 0.87 for unintentional invaders, success decoupled from residence time) establishing chiefly through urbanization of former croplands and coniferous forests into wetland/coastal/riparian fringes, whereas fully built-up, long-urban plots are instead dominated by unintentionally introduced ruderal annuals (Erigeron, Amaranthus, Xanthium spp., broad niche breadth).

native_result.query: What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use influenced plant introductions both historically and ecologically: the urbanization era (post-1900, especially post-1985) shifted the dominant introduction pathway toward ornamental/gardening introductions (16.8% of introductions before 1500 vs 75.2% in 1985-2019; χ²=230.4, p=6e-47), while at the landscape scale increasing urban cover around plots shifts the composition of established aliens toward unintentionally introduced, ruderal, broad-niche herbs (Unintentional share 51%→68% across urban-cover bins, χ²=19.9, p=0.003; presence OR=1.5-1.9 per SD urban cover) and excludes agriculture/forestry introductions (0 aliens in the most urbanized plots), with gardening aliens persisting mainly in progressively changed peri-urban coastal and wetland habitats rather than dense urban cores.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Temporal: χ² and shares on the 4-period × 3-pathway contingency table. 2) Plot-level (191/632 invaded plots): Spearman correlations of pathway proportions/richness vs urban cover (3 years × 3 buffers), pooled pathway × urban-bin χ², binned pathway shares, logistic presence GLMs (z-scored urban, elevation, temperature) with scale sensitivity (50/500/1000 m), landscape-change correlations, supplementary Poisson richness models, habitat summary. 3) Species-level (77 species after dedup): pathway means and Kruskal-Wallis for invaded plots/niche breadth/habitat range/mrt, growth-form × pathway crosstab, family profile; phylogeny verified (81 tips = species labels) but kept as secondary family-level note. native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use changed not just how many introduced plants invade but which types: rising urban cover increases invader richness overall, and progressive urban+cropland expansion (1956–2009) shifts the invader community toward Gardening-origin (ornamental) introductions (RR 1.18, p=0.003), mirroring the regional historical shift from AgriForest-dominated (51% before 1500) to Gardening-dominated (75% in 1985–2019) introduction pools. Unintentional invaders concentrate in long-established high-urban contexts (urban cover RR 1.12, p=0.047; expansion RR 0.89, p=0.022) and have broader invaded niches and higher plot occupancy than gardening species after controlling for residence time; AgriForest introductions are rare, trend away from urban plots, and are underpowered. Pathway membership is phylogenetically clustered (p<0.002) but invasion success shows no phylogenetic signal (λ≈0.12, p=0.71), so the urban–pathway associations are not confounded by shared ancestry.
native_result.WorkflowB: A: χ² on 4×3 period×pathway table. B1: NB GLM of per-plot invader counts (n=632) on urban/cropland 2009 cover + 1956–2009 progressive/regressive change, controls for elevation/climate/roads/streams, sensitivity across 50/500/1000 m buffers (1000 m primary). B2: pathway composition among 191 invaded plots via Poisson GLM with log(n.total) offset and HC1 SEs (binomial models discarded for quasi-complete separation). B3: habitat and urban-median contrasts. B4: Moran's I permutation test on residuals. C: 77 deduplicated species; Kruskal–Wallis + NB model of plots-invaded ~ pathway + mrt. D: manual Newick parse, cophenetic distances, Pagel's λ MLE + LR tests, 999-permutation pathway-clustering test; PGLS omitted because λ≈0. E: coefficient-grounded synthesis.

The absolute attenuation gap is similar for Cognitive (mean −0.23; meta-analytic −0.23 [−0.33, −0.14]) and Social psychology (−0.20; meta-analytic −0.22 [−0.29, −0.15]) and somewhat smaller in Economics (−0.24; meta-analytic −0.13 [−0.25, −0.01], p = 0.03, n = 18). On the relative scale, however, Social psychology shows the strongest attenuation (median relative effect size 0.13, i.e., replications recover only ~13% of the original effect) compared with Cognitive (0.65) and Economics (0.70), because Social original effects are smallest in absolute terms. native_result.HypoA: Studies in Experimental Economics tend to have longer original papers compared to Psychology. The average length of original papers in Experimental Economics is 28 pages, whereas in Psychology, the average is 11 pages.
native_result.HypoB: Original papers in Experimental Economics are on average much longer than those in Psychology: EERP originals (project=='ee') average 28.0 pages (n=18, median 27.5) versus 11.2 pages for RPP originals (project=='rpp', deduplicated to n=95 unique papers, median 9.0) — roughly a 2.5× difference (~16.8 pages), reflecting economics journals' long-article format versus psychology's short articles.

native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality increased within both white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort, in the form of polarization rather than uniform spread: mean composite wealth rose (males $88,163->$131,792; females $99,605->$128,837, nominal USD) while medians fell sharply (males $15,601->$8,900; females $20,100->$8,825) and the zero-wealth share grew from ~26% to ~43% in both groups. The upper tail pulled away from the middle: P90/P50 nearly tripled (males 13.8->37.5; females 12.1->37.6) and the overall Gini rose modestly (males 0.781->0.794; females 0.763->0.778), while the top-decile share stayed flat (~0.62 males, ~0.59 females). native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 extract, there is no Black advantage in college-enrollment/BA-track attainment (ever recorded in a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence in 1981–1983; no post-1979 education variable exists in the data, so literal BA completion cannot be measured) at any socioeconomic status level. The Black–non-Black/non-Hispanic gap is essentially zero among low-SES families (+0.6 pp, n.s.), small at mid SES (−1.5 pp, n.s.), and large at high SES (−10.1 pp, p<0.0001), with a significant race×SES interaction (LRT=12.14, p=0.0023; Black×High-SES OR=0.29). Hypothesis: each increment of family SES yields substantially larger BA-track attainment gains for non-Black/non-Hispanic respondents than for Black respondents, so racial parity in BA-track attainment exists only at the bottom of the SES distribution and racial disparities are widest among the most advantaged families; the pattern is specific to the Black–non-Black/non-Hispanic contrast (Hispanic respondents reach near-parity at high SES, 19.4% vs 16.8%).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 rows × 61 columns). Cleaned NLSY sentinel codes (≥90) in education to missing; retained negative family net wealth as valid negative net worth (signed-log transform); income had no negative codes. Outcome: binary college-enrollment/BA-track proxy = residence code 3 (dorm/frat/sorority) in any of 1981–1983 (1,017 positive; 42.5% positive in >1 wave), explicitly a proxy because the file's only education variable is 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (respondents then aged 14–22). SES: composite index = mean of z(max of mother's/father's highest grade completed) and z(log 1979 total net family income), split into tertiles; strict complete cases retained (9,904/12,686 = 78.1%). Primary evidence: Black-vs-non-Black/non-Hispanic enrollment-rate gap within each SES tertile, and logistic regression colEnroll ~ black × SES-tertile + sex + age79 with LRT for the interaction; Hispanic cohort (n=2,402) reported separately throughout. Sensitivities: income-only quartiles; wealth-added composite (adds signed-log 1985 net wealth, flagged nonrandom subset n=7,934); winsorized top-1% income; missing-SES indicator category. All computations in analysis.py; tables exported to outputs/.

native_result.query: Is the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines of the individual?
native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: SES is positively associated with BA-degree completion within every racial group in this NLS sample (n = 8,773; 236 completions), but its strength does not differ significantly across racial lines on the relative (odds) scale: after controlling for sex and family size, the SES log-odds slope is statistically indistinguishable between White respondents (OR 1.74), Black respondents (OR ≈2.37, SES×race interaction p = 0.09) and Hispanic respondents (OR ≈1.95, p = 0.63); the interactions are jointly non-significant (LR χ²(2) = 2.58, p = 0.28) and per-race stratified fits are statistically equal (SES ORs 1.82 / 2.18 / 1.82; equality Wald tests p ≥ 0.33). What racial lines do change is the payoff in absolute probability: because baseline completion is far lower for Black (1.3%) and Hispanic (1.4%) than White (3.5%) respondents, a one-SD SES advantage raises predicted completion probability by only ~0.9–1.0 percentage points for Black and Hispanic respondents versus ~2.3 points for White respondents (bootstrap 95% CIs for the minority-minus-White contrasts exclude zero: [−2.15, −0.84] and [−2.16, −0.73] pp). Net of the SES-linked academic-resources pathway (composite ASVAB and class percentile), the SES gradient shrinks for all groups and the negative racial main effects disappear, indicating ability and class standing are the principal channel through which SES and race jointly affect degree completion. Thus racial lines affect the SES→degree relation mainly by lowering the baseline — and hence the absolute return to SES — for Black and Hispanic respondents, not through a detectably different relative SES slope; with only 19–28 completion events in the minority groups, modest slope differences cannot be ruled out. Caveats: the follow-up window defining 'BA completed' is not documented, and no sampling weights are supplied, so findings describe this processed sample.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows × 8 columns; zero missing values, zero duplicate CASE IDs). Verified SES is continuous (5,753 distinct values, range −2.45..2.72; not banded), race has 3 levels (White 5,337 / Black 2,113 / Hispanic 1,323), sex is binary, and BA DEGREE COMPLETED has 236 positives (2.69%). Standardized SES and the ASVAB composite and scaled class percentile to [0,1]. Fit three nested logistic regressions (M1: SES+race+SES×race; M2: +sex+family size — headline; M3: +ASVAB z +class percentile — labeled net-of-academic-resources comparison) with HC1 robust SEs, plus a joint LR test of the interactions. Estimated average marginal effects of +1 SD SES within each race by the delta method and percentile bootstrap (1,000 reps, fixed seed) for racial contrasts, and predicted probabilities at SES quartiles. Robustness: linear probability model; cubic SES; SES standardized within race; Firth penalized logit (rare-event check); per-race stratified logits with cross-equation Wald equality tests. Treated ability/class rank as part of the SES pathway per study direction. All estimates are observational associations; unweighted (no weights supplied); follow-up timing undocumented.

native_result.HypoA: Project leads (49.6%, 95% CI [49.219, 49.981]) and data scientists (61.389%, 95% CI [60.955, 61.822]) have the highest proportion of association with requirements in ML-enabled systems after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: The two roles with the highest proportion of association with requirements in ML-enabled systems are the Project Lead / Project Manager (51.03% of 194 usable respondents, 95% bootstrap CI [43.81, 58.25]) and the Data Scientist (48.97%, 95% CI [42.27, 55.67]), well ahead of Business Analyst (25.77%), Developer (19.07%), Solution Architect (12.37%), Requirements Engineer (10.31%) and Tester (1.03%). Requirements-related ML concerns concentrate in the managerial (Project Lead) and technical (Data Scientist) poles of the delivery pipeline; the ordering between the two is a statistical near-tie (paired bootstrap P(Lead>Scientist)=0.642, and it flips in the Completed-only sensitivity variant), but their joint top-2 status is stable in 100% of 10,000 bootstrap replicates and in all sensitivity analyses. The supplied reference proportions (49.6%, CI [49.219, 49.981]; 61.389%, CI [60.955, 61.822]) could not be reproduced from this data: their CI widths imply an effective sample of ~50-65k, incompatible with any respondent-level bootstrap of n=194 (honest CIs are ±~7 pp); the Completed-only variant yields 49.39% for both top roles, inside the first reference CI.

native_result.query: Which technique is considered the most commonly used by respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 69.399% indicating so (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: Interviews (69.399% respondents saying so, 95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) are the most commonly used technique considered by the respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: Interviews are the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: they were quoted (used) by 97 of 194 valid respondents (50.0%, 95% bootstrap CI [42.8%, 57.2%]), ranking first ahead of Scenarios and Prototyping (38.7% each), Workshops/Meetings (38.1%), Observation (33.0%) and Other techniques (5.7%). This ranking is robust to weighting the sample by project exposure: weighting respondents by their total number of ML projects (D7) raises Interviews to 74.0% (CI [61.3%, 83.5%]) and weighting by deployed ML projects (D8) yields 68.2% (CI [56.7%, 78.2%]; naive project-expanded CI [64.5%, 71.9%]). The deployed-project-weighted estimate (68.197%) is the closest grounded figure to the referenced benchmark of 69.399% (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]), which is treated as an external anchor only — its CI width (~±0.34 pp) implies ~72,000 bootstrap units and cannot be reproduced from 276 respondents (or 1,344 respondent-project pairs).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Load CSV (276x202); 2) clean: drop -77 Q-blocks (valid N=194), treat -99/-66/negative Duration as non-response; 3) binarize Q9 'quoted'=uses technique; 4) compute per-technique proportions unweighted and weighted by D7_Total_ML_Projects / D8_ML_Production; 5) respondent-level cluster bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 42) for percentile 95% CIs per scheme; 6) sensitivity: (a) exclude all 88 suspended (N=188), (b) add Q9_Others_Free text mentions; 7) project-expanded (respondent-project pair) replication check with naive bootstrap; 8) identify rank-1 technique per scheme and the proportion nearest the 69.399% benchmark anchor; 9) emit natural-language hypothesis. Outputs: analysis/elicitation_analysis.py, analysis/q9_proportions_bootstrap.csv.

native_result.query: Which two documentation formats are the least used for requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 10.13% (95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and 4.366% (95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) of respondents indicating so, respectively, after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: The least used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are ML Canvas (10.13% respondents, 95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) Scenarios (4.366% respondents, 95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: The two least-used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are BDD scenarios (4/194 = 2.06%, bootstrap 95% CI [0.52%, 4.12%]) and the ML Canvas (15/194 = 7.73%, 95% CI [4.12%, 11.86%]). Practitioners rarely adopt these structured/ML-specific notations, defaulting instead to notebooks (34.02%), user stories (32.47%) and requirements lists (26.29%). Caveats reported transparently: the free-text catch-all 'Others' category ties ML Canvas exactly (15/194, CI [4.12%, 11.86%]) and is treated as a non-named format; ML Canvas is statistically tied with Vision Documents/Goal Models (14.95%) within bootstrap uncertainty. The stated target percentages (10.13% and 4.366%, with ±0.2 pp CIs) could not be reproduced from the supplied binary quoted/not-quoted data under any tested aggregation (denominator 276/194/174/416, share-of-total-selections, inverse-frequency weighting, bootstrap means, exhaustive fraction search); they most likely derive from the original study's ordinal degree-of-use coding, which is not present in this CSV. The rank ordering itself is robust across all tested aggregations.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded the 276x202 CSV; confirmed all 12 substantive Q10_ML_Documentation_* columns are binary categorical ('quoted'/'not quoted'/'-77'), not Likert. 2) Excluded the 82 respondents with the -77 skip sentinel (aligned with Status='Suspended'), leaving n=194. 3) Coded usage as a binary indicator ('quoted') and computed per-format usage rates. 4) Bootstrapped the 194 respondents with replacement, B=10,000, seed=42, percentile 95% CIs. 5) Ranked formats ascending; identified BDD Scenarios (2.06%) and ML Canvas (7.73%) as least used, handling the MLCanvas/Others tie in favor of the named format and reporting it explicitly. 6) Ran a reconciliation pass against the target percentages testing five alternative aggregations (denominator 276 with -77 as non-use; share of 416 total quoted selections; denominator of 174 respondents quoting >=1 format; inverse-frequency weighting; exhaustive small-fraction search plus bootstrap-mean comparison) — none reproduces both 10.13% and 4.366% or their narrow CIs, so the answer is grounded in the computed rates and the aggregation-invariant rank ordering.

native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Across 1975–2015, rising per capita income (GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$) in both Sub-Saharan Africa and lower-middle-income countries coincided with a declining education-expenditure share of GNI, so that — measured associationally, with lagged expenditure, group trends and HAC/AR(1) errors — the estimated effect of education expenditure on per capita income is not positive in either group: in the 2011–2015 window where SSA income is observed, a 1 percentage-point-of-GNI higher lagged education share is associated with roughly 0.04–0.11 log points (~4–11%) lower per capita income in SSA versus roughly 0.36–0.73 log points (~36–73%) lower in LMC, i.e. the negative association is consistently flatter in SSA — approximately one-sixth to one-eighth the LMC magnitude — and the raw SSA-vs-LMC difference is nominally significant (Wald p<0.001) but does not survive AR(1) or first-difference specifications; therefore the defensible hypothesis is that the income association with education expenditure is similarly weak (effectively zero after accounting for trends) in both groups, with no detectable SSA–LMC difference in the education-spending–income relationship, and SSA's consistently flatter slope suggesting, at most, a smaller negative association rather than a distinct positive effect.
native_result.WorkflowB: Tidied the WB wide CSV (12 rows = 6 series × 2 groups, 41 year columns; empty cells = missing, no '..' markers) into a group-year panel. Outcome: GNI per capita constant 2015 US$ (NY.GNP.PCAP.KD; file supersedes the brief's 'per capita GDP 2010 US$'). Treatment: adjusted savings education expenditure, % of GNI (NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS). Controls: gross primary/secondary enrollment, export growth, labor force participation (1991–2015 coverage). Main model: log GNI pc on lagged (t−1) education expenditure, LMC dummy, LMC×expenditure interaction, group-specific trends, HAC(Newey-West)/GLS-AR(1) errors; gamma (interaction) is the SSA-vs-LMC comparison, tested by Wald. SSA income is observed only 2011–2015 (5/41 years), so the income comparison runs on the 2011–2015 overlap (N=10) and SSA is additionally routed through the enrollment channel over the full 1975–2015 window (SSA income not imputed). Robustness (exactly four checks): levels vs first differences; balanced 1991–2015 window; exclusion of crisis years 2008–2010; HAC vs AR(1) errors. All coefficients collapse toward zero and lose significance under AR(1)/FD; group difference significant only in raw levels. Caveats: group-level aggregates only (N=2 units), small-sample HAC unreliable at N=10, LMC is a narrow proxy for 'developing countries', associational not causal.

native_result.HypoB: Older respondents are less likely to withdraw more from savings than they put in: each additional year of age (24-32) is associated with ~9% lower odds of dissaving (adjusted OR 0.915, 95% CI 0.896-0.934, p<0.001; unadjusted OR 0.891), with adjusted predicted withdrawal probability falling from ~46% at age 24 to ~29% at age 32. The relationship is essentially linear (centered AGE^2 OR 0.985, p=0.003 - statistically significant but negligible curvature). Critical caveat: 31.2% of rows have mean-imputed income (their share rises from 27% at age 24 to 45% at age 32, and they withdraw far less often: 11.2% vs 29.2%), so the gradient is largely compositional; among respondents with observed income the age effect vanishes (adjusted OR 0.999, p=0.93; unadjusted OR 0.987, p=0.28; withdrawal rates flat at ~48-54%). The cross-sectional negative age gradient is therefore best read as 'older respondents dissave less', robust to covariate adjustment and comparison-group definition, but substantially attributable to age-related income missingness rather than a clean aging effect.

native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration simultaneously increases in the 17th century BCE — the century bin CE −1700 to −1601 (1700–1601 BCE). At that bin PotteryForm drops from z = +0.74 to z = −1.13 (Δz ≈ −1.87) and stays on this plateau for 13 centuries (to CE −500), while PotteryDecoration jumps from z = −0.48 to z = +0.97 (Δz ≈ +1.45) in the same century. This is the unique century in the 37-bin series (CE −4100…−500) where a form collapse (|Δz| ≥ 1, level crossing zero downward, sustained ≥ 3 centuries) coincides with a decoration increase (|Δz| ≥ 1, level crossing zero upward, sustained ≥ 3 centuries); the result is stable to threshold choices and reproduced by a 100-year rolling mean on the annual interpolated series. The later decoration rise at CE −1000 (+0.56, to z = 1.53) is NOT simultaneous (form unchanged at −1.13), and the other large form shift (−2900 → −2800) is accompanied by a decoration decrease, not an increase.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded and cross-validated three CSVs: time_series_data.csv (3601 annual rows, CE −4100…−500; raw PotteryForm/PotteryDecoration at 37 century marks, piecewise-constant; _inter annual, 0 NaN; CE+calBP=1950 check passed), capital.csv (BCE 500–4300, decimal=',', CE=−BCE; values identical to time_series at all 37 overlapping years, max abs diff 0.0), pollen file (context only, coverage ends CE −702, not used for dating). 2) Unit of analysis: 100-year bins matching native resolution of the raw z series. 3) Formal detection: collapse = Δz ≤ −1.0 vs previous bin AND level < 0 AND sustained ≥ 3 centuries; increase = Δz ≥ +1.0 AND level > 0 AND sustained ≥ 3 centuries. 4) Simultaneity = same century bin is both events; fallback = overlapping event intervals. 5) Sensitivity grid (Δz 1.0/1.5 × sustain 3/5) — no configuration yields any other simultaneous bin. 6) Independent cross-check: 100-year centered rolling mean on annual PotteryForm_inter/PotteryDecoration_inter — largest form drop at bin −1700 with decoration rising (+0.706); first CE with rolling decoration > +0.5 is −1730, inside the −1700 bin. 7) Full inventory of all 37 bins saved to pottery_bins_table.csv showing uniqueness of the −1700 event.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.

sub_hypo.text: Pottery Form diversity collapses while Pottery Decoration diversity increases in the same 17th-century BCE bin, CE −1700 to −1601. PotteryForm falls from +0.74 to −1.13 (Δz ≈ −1.87), remaining at −1.13 for 13 centuries through CE −500, while PotteryDecoration rises from −0.48 to +0.97 (Δz ≈ +1.45).

sub_hypo.text: Gardening introductions constitute a larger share of invaded non-native flora in wetlands, coastal habitats and forests than in croplands and urban habitats, where unintentional introductions dominate.
sub_hypo.context: Non-native flora in Barcelona province; 481 invaded-species records grouped by habitat. Forest estimates are based on sparse samples of at most 8 records.
sub_hypo.relations: Gardening share (n.gard/n.total) is approximately 56% in wetlands, 53% in coastal habitats and 88–100% in forest plots, compared with 19% in croplands and 30% in urban plots. Unintentional introductions dominate croplands and urban habitats. Pathway and habitat are associated (chi-square=75.2, df=18, permutation p=0.0002; 10,000 permutations with habitat margins fixed). Gardening share is modeled with a Firth-penalized logistic GLM using croplands as the reference habitat.

sub_hypo.text: Despite their lower proportional representation in urban habitats, gardening species are most frequent in absolute per-plot terms in urban, coastal, wetland and riparian plots, which are the most heavily invaded habitats overall; croplands are dominated by unintentional introductions.
sub_hypo.context: All 632 sampled plots in Barcelona province, including plots without gardening introductions.
sub_hypo.relations: Urban, coastal, wetland and riparian habitats have 0.6–0.8 gardening records per plot, gardening presence in 36–50% of plots, and overall invasion frequencies of 1.4–2.3 records per plot. Thus, absolute gardening frequency and proportional gardening share give different habitat comparisons. Gardening presence (n.gard>0) is modeled with a Firth-penalized logistic GLM using croplands as the reference habitat.

sub_hypo.text: Pathway estimates for rock outcrops, scrublands and both forest types are unstable because they are based on at most 8 records.
sub_hypo.context: Sparse habitat groups among the sampled non-native flora in Barcelona province; these habitats are flagged rather than collapsed.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Non-native plants introduced via gardening make up a markedly larger share of the invaded non-native flora in wet, coastal and forested habitats than in croplands and urban habitats: gardening accounts for ~56% of non-native records in wetlands, ~53% in coastal habitats and ~88-100% in forest plots (sparse, <=8 records), versus ~19% in croplands and ~30% in urban plots, where unintentional introductions dominate (chi2=75.2, df=18, permutation p=0.0002). In absolute per-plot terms the views diverge: gardening species are most frequent in urban, coastal, wetland and riparian plots (0.6-0.8 records/plot; present in 36-50% of plots) because these habitats are most heavily invaded overall (1.4-2.3 records/plot), while croplands are dominated by unintentional introductions. Estimates for rock outcrops, scrublands and both forest types rest on <=8 records and are unstable.

native_result.query: In what context does the gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants show different prevalence styles across habitat types?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway shows two qualitatively different prevalence styles across habitat types, and the distinguishing context is the degree of human modification of the habitat. In strongly anthropogenic, high-richness habitats (Urban, Croplands, and to a lesser extent Riparian), gardening operates in an absolute-flux style: it contributes the largest raw numbers of non-native plant records (45 in Urban, 35 in Riparian, 29 in Wetlands, 23 in Coastal), but it coexists with — and in Urban (29.8% of records) and Croplands (18.5%) is outnumbered by — a dominant unintentional introduction flux. In natural, low-richness habitats (Broad-leaved and Coniferous forests, secondarily Wetlands and Coastal), gardening operates in a conditional-dominance style: very few non-natives establish (4 records across 68 broad-leaved forest plots; 8 across 77 coniferous plots), yet when any non-native occurs it is almost always a gardening introduction (100% in Broad-leaved forests, 87.5% in Coniferous forests, >50% in Wetlands and Coastal), with the unintentional pathway virtually absent there (0 records in both forest types). This is consistent with gardening species being habitat specialists — lower invaded niche breadth (median 0.36 vs 0.87), fewer invaded plots (median 2 vs 3), and smaller habitat range (mean 2.0 vs 2.7) than unintentionally introduced species — concentrating where planted (gardens, urban/riparian settings, wetland and coastal edges) and spilling into natural forests as nearly the sole non-native source, while unintentional weeds spread broadly across disturbed anthropogenic habitats. Secondary temporal context: gardening's regional share rose from 16.8% (before 1500) to 75.2% (1985–2019), implying a growing gardening-dominated signature in natural forests. In marginal habitats (Rock outcrops: 0 gardening records; Scrublands: 2 records, 2.8% occupancy) neither style applies. This is a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a demonstrated causal mechanism.

native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted the invasion type associated with UNINTENTIONAL introduction (contaminant/hitchhiker weeds) rather than ornamental Gardening escapees: controlling for habitat, cropland and elevation, higher urban cover around plots shifts the pathway mix toward Unintentional invaders (Gardening-vs-Unintentional urban contrast b=-1.15, SE 0.54, p=0.032 at urban.2009.50m; direction negative in 9/9 buffer-year combinations, significant in 6/9, strongest at 500-1000 m buffers, e.g. -2.80, p=0.009 at urban.1956.500m). In Urban-habitat plots the Unintentional share of invaders is 68.9% vs 29.8% Gardening. Unintentionally introduced species also occupy broader invaded niches (median 0.83 vs 0.38, KW p=0.047) and more plots (phylogeny-corrected PGLS b=+1.44, p<0.001), although Gardening dominates the introduction pool temporally (share 17%->75% of introductions, 1985-2019 vs Before-1500; chi2=230.4, p<1e-46). Scenario: urban land use - contemporary cover (2009) and cumulative landscape-scale urban presence (>=500 m buffers) - filters establishment in favour of unintentionally introduced, niche-broad generalists over garden-escape ornamentals.

native_result.query: What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use influences plant introductions primarily by increasing the overall incidence of non-native plants rather than by selectively shifting which introduction pathway dominates: plots embedded in urbanized landscapes are far more likely to host non-native plants at all (mean urban cover 0.27 vs 0.04, 2009/50 m), but pathway composition within invaded plots is only weakly and non-robustly related to urban cover. Suggestive, non-significant signals — a hump-shaped mid-urban peak in Gardening records relative to Unintentional ones (urban² p=0.13), a positive urban effect on Gardening in the all-plots model (OR 6.45, p=0.078), and a positive association with progressive 1956–2009 urbanization (OR 3.1, p=0.34) — together with the century-scale rise of the Gardening share of introductions (17% before 1500 to 75% in 1985–2019) are consistent with long-term urbanization favoring ornamental (Gardening) introductions, but plot-level evidence does not support a strong pathway-specific urban effect.
native_result.WorkflowB: Parsed invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, tab-separated; verified n.total = n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo, 481 records: Gardening 169, Unintentional 289, AgriForest 23). Fit multinomial logistic regressions with cluster-robust SEs by plot, baseline Unintentional: Model A presence-only (191 plots/481 records) and Model B all 632 plots with an 'Absent' category, both reported per researcher instruction; both diverge at 2009/50m (A: −1.42, p=0.098; B: +1.86, p=0.078). Sensitivity across 9 year×buffer combos (1956/1993/2009 × 50/500/1000 m): no significant urban effect in any combo (0/9 in both models), signs flip — not robust. Model C with landscape-change covariates: progressive 1956–2009 change OR=3.1 (p=0.34) for Gardening vs Unintentional; C2 unstable (Hessian inversion failed) and excluded from conclusions. Corroboration: Catalonia contingency table shows Gardening share rising 0.168→0.752; phylo note: 81/81 tip-label match, Gardening species across 30/33 families. Outputs: outputs/results.xlsx.

native_result.query: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use acts as a pathway-specific filter on plant invasion rather than a uniform amplifier: increasing urban cover at 500–1000 m buffers strongly excludes AgriForest-origin invaders (β=−2.34, p=0.002) and relatively favors Gardening (+1.84, p=0.022) and Unintentional (+2.42, p=0.0015) introductions, driven by a regional propagule-pool shift toward ornamental introductions (Gardening share of first records 17% pre-1500 → 75% post-1985) and pathway-linked traits (Unintentional species are annual herbs with broad native niches, KW p=0.0015; AgriForest species are cultivation shrubs/trees). The effect is landscape-scale (absent at 50 m), tied to static urban cover rather than recent urbanization dynamics, and specific to urban (not cropland) cover.
native_result.WorkflowB: Pandas inspection -> long-format Poisson GLM (count ~ pathway x urban.2009.500m + cropland + habitat + elevation + climate + distances; cluster-robust by plot; NB robustness) -> per-pathway supporting GLMs -> AgriForest presence/absence binomial GLM as robustness -> interaction-coefficient sensitivity grid over 9 buffer/year combinations -> VIF/collinearity check -> compositional landscape-change models -> species-level trait contrasts on 77 de-duplicated species (Kruskal-Wallis + chi-square) -> temporal share summary. Script: analysis.py; outputs in results/.

native_result.query: For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Original-study effect size estimates tend to be larger than replication estimates in all three domains — Social, Cognitive, and Economics — and by a similar amount (mean original-minus-replication deficit on the Fisher-z scale: Cognitive +0.29, Economics +0.27, Social +0.23; originals are larger in magnitude in ~85% of studies: Social 88%, Economics 83%, Cognitive 82%). The domains do not differ reliably from one another (omnibus permutation p=0.76; all pairwise 95% CIs include 0), so the data support 'original effects are larger than replications everywhere' rather than any domain-specific hierarchy. Under precision weighting, the deficit remains clear for Cognitive and Social (~+0.21 each) but is not distinguishable from zero for Economics (+0.01, CI [-0.08, 0.20]), and Economics shows the highest median replication-to-original ratio (0.70 vs 0.65 Cognitive and ~0.13-0.18 Social). Caveat: domain is fully confounded with replication project (Social/Cognitive = RPP only, n=34 each; Economics = EERP only, n=18), so domain and project effects cannot be separated, and the Economics estimate rests on only 18 studies.

native_result.query: What kind of demographic disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated?
native_result.HypoA: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 respondents who were ever incarcerated (ever_jailed=1, jailed sometime in 1985-1994), 1985 wealth is sharply demographically stratified. The most robust disparity is racial, among men: white men held a median of $2,000 (n=57), roughly 2.5x the Black-male median ($800, n=143; gap -$1,200) and ~2.9x the Hispanic-male median ($700, n=52; gap -$1,300). The starkest disparity is by sex within minority groups: Black and Hispanic women who were ever incarcerated had median wealth of $0 - an absence of assets rather than debts (0% negative values among Black women) - with 78-81% reporting exactly zero wealth, versus $700-$800 for same-race men. White women (n=12) show the numerically highest median ($4,100, +$2,100 vs white men), but this small cell is not headline material. As background contrast, the pooled ever-incarcerated median ($720, n=289) sits far below the never-incarcerated median ($3,600, n=11,724). Caveats: ever_jailed spans 1985-1994, so 1985 wealth may predate or postdate incarceration for part of the group - the pattern is a descriptive association, not causal; 5.4% of 1985 wealth values are negative (net debts) and 26.7% are exactly zero, so medians near zero partly reflect the mass at zero; medians are not fully stable to full-row deduplication (shifts up to $1,300, narrowing the Hispanic-male deficit), and small female cells (n=9-16) make within-race sex gaps suggestive rather than definitive.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows, 6 cols, 0 missing; race value typo 'hipanic' kept as-is in data, reported as Hispanic in prose). Diagnostics: composite_wealth_1985 spans -$57,587 to $2,574,706 with 649 negatives (5.4%, net-of-debt composite) and 3,209 zeros (26.7%); 2,056 rows in 157 exact-duplicate groups (largest 617 rows), retained in main analysis with dedup sensitivity rerun; no residence or timing columns exist, so the residence-based incarceration proxy could not be applied and ever_jailed (binary, 289 ever = 2.4%) was taken at face value. Main analysis: ever_jailed=1 subset grouped by race x sex; median/mean/zero-share/neg-share per cell; dollar gaps and ratios vs reference white male; full 15-pair pairwise comparisons with ratios only where reference median > $0. Background: same breakdown for ever_jailed=0. Sensitivity: full-row dedup shifts medians up to $1,300 (black male 800->1,400, hipanic male 700->2,000, white male 2,000->2,100; female zero-medians unchanged). Conclusions ordered: male race gaps first, then sex-within-race, then small-cell and zero-median caveats; conclusions resting on n<15 not headlined.

native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration between 1985 and 1994 is associated with worse wealth outcomes at every baseline-wealth tier, with the damage concentrated proportionally at the bottom: jailed respondents who began with low positive wealth (<= $5,300) typically lost all of it by 1996 (median relative change -100%, ending at median $0) while comparable non-jailed respondents grew wealth roughly five-fold (+525%); in the zero-wealth tier jailed respondents accumulated essentially nothing (jailed men ~$7,900 vs ~$18,500 mean accumulation) and in the highest positive tier jailed men saw median wealth decline ~$7,000-8,000 vs a ~$12,500 gain for non-jailed peers. Sex-adjusted regressions find a significant negative jailed coefficient in every tier (p <= 0.02). In absolute dollars the shortfall grows with baseline wealth (DiD-style gaps: -1,948 / 0 / -7,770 / -14,775 across tiers), but the cross-tier interaction is not statistically significant (p = 0.07-0.17), so the tier gradient in levels is descriptive. All statements are associations, not causal effects.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected data (12,013 rows x 6 cols, no missing values, no ID; wide format; wealth can be negative). 2) Restricted to black respondents (n=3,013; 159 jailed, 5.3%; male 9.8% vs female 1.0%). 3) Winsorized wealth levels at black-sample 1st/99th percentiles per wave (62 rows/wave affected; 31 extreme-negative rows per wave flagged, not dropped). 4) Built primary baseline (1985) tiers negative/zero/positive-low/positive-high using the median of positive 1985 wealth ($5,300) because terciles/quartiles degenerate at 0; quartile variant run as sensitivity. 5) Computed absolute changes 1985->1990 and 1985->1996, relative changes for positive baselines, and 1996 levels. 6) Compared jailed vs not-jailed within every tier x sex cell via medians, winsorized means, and Mann-Whitney U tests (both cells >= 5); reported jailed/non-jailed counts per tier x sex. 7) Pooled within-tier sex-adjusted OLS (HC3) of change 1985->1996 on jailed + male. 8) DiD-style jail gaps in change by tier and cross-tier jail x tier interaction OLS. 9) Stated associational caveats: coarse 1985-1994 ever_jailed proxy with unmeasured timing/severity; non-random selection into incarceration; unknown composite-wealth construction; no income variable so baseline wealth proxies income; tiny female jailed cells; unmeasurable attrition; possible extreme-debt coding artifacts.

native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 youth, the racial gap in early college-track attainment (completing 13+ grades by 1979, the closest feasible proxy for eventual BA completion, which is not directly recorded in this extract) does not follow a uniform pattern across SES: Black respondents in the low-SES tercile attain college-track status at rates equal to or higher than non-Black peers (4.8% vs 4.1%, RR=1.19), but the advantage reverses with rising SES (high tercile: 18.5% vs 21.4%, RR=0.87), and against non-Black non-Hispanic peers the Black advantage at low SES (RR=1.48) shrinks to a deficit at high SES (logistic Black x SES interaction -0.36, p=0.006). SES raises college-track attainment for both groups, but the marginal return to SES is larger for non-Black respondents, so the racial gap WIDENS as SES rises. We hypothesize this diminishing-return pattern carries over to eventual BA completion, which the supplied data could not verify.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_raw.csv (12,686x61); cleaned grade codes 0/95 as missing; outcome A = grade>=13 by 1979 (primary), outcome B = grade>=12 (consistency); SES composite = mean pooled percentile of log 1979 family income, max parental grade, reversed family size, split into race-pooled terciles; Black vs non-Black pooled rates and gaps with 95% CIs and risk ratios per tercile; sensitivity: ages>=19 subset, complete-case and median-imputed SES, Black vs non-Black-non-Hispanic only; logistic regressions race + ses_tercile + race x ses + male + age79; interaction stability summarized across 7 specifications.

native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: С 1985 года медианное семейное чистое богатство у респондентов NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC (трактованных как прокси white) стабильно выше, чем у BLACK и HISPANIC, и разрыв со временем растёт: в 1985 медианы $3,500 (white) vs $1,600 (black) vs $500 (Hispanic), к 1996 — $42,600 vs $9,800 vs $2,562.5. Отношение white/black выросло с 2.2x до 4.35x, white/Hispanic — с 7.0x до 16.6x. Hispanic-группа имеет наихудшую медиану во все годы и наибольшую долю нулевого wealth (~19–34%), black-группа растёт быстрее в абсолюте, но отстаёт в 2–4.7 раза. Вывод устойчив к attrition: на сбалансированной панели (n=5,739) те же выводы с ratios 2.4x–17.8x. Оговорки: значения номинальные; негативы — реальные долги, нули — реальный нулевой wealth (сохранены); выборка с неполным откликом — к 1996 остаётся ~56% исходной, группа white-прокси теряет 38% против ~20% у minority-групп, что может смещать медианы 1996 года, но чувствительность-проверка показывает, что направление вывода не меняется.

sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents with nonmissing wealth in 1985, 1990, or 1996, analyzed separately by year; nominal negative and zero wealth values are retained.

sub_hypo.text: The direction of the racial/ethnic wealth differences and their widening over time persists in a balanced panel of 5,739 respondents, with white/minority median wealth ratios ranging from 2.4 to 17.8.
sub_hypo.context: Sensitivity analysis restricted to NLSY79 respondents with nonmissing family net wealth in all three years: 1985, 1990, and 1996. Nominal values, including debts and zeros, are retained.
sub_hypo.relations: Restricting analysis to the balanced panel preserves the wealth ordering and widening disparities observed in the available-response sample.

sub_hypo.text: Wealth-response attrition differs by racial/ethnic group: retention from 1985 to 1996 is 80.5% for BLACK respondents, 80.3% for HISPANIC respondents, and 61.6% for the white-proxy group. By 1996, approximately 56% of the original sample remains. Greater white-proxy attrition may bias 1996 medians, although the balanced-panel sensitivity analysis preserves the direction of the conclusions.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 wealth-response availability, including group-specific retention from 1985 to 1996 and comparison with the original sample.
sub_hypo.relations: White-proxy respondents have lower retention and greater attrition than BLACK and HISPANIC respondents; potential attrition bias does not reverse the observed disparities in the balanced-panel check.

native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: SES is positively associated with BA completion by the observation date (pooled OR 1.34/unit, 95% CI 1.07-1.67, p=0.010; +1 SD SES = +0.44 pp on a 2.7% base rate), but after adjustment for sex, family size, ASVAB ability and class percentile, the joint 2-df SES x race interaction test is not significant (chi2(2)=1.75, p=0.42), so the data provide no detectable evidence that the SES-completion gradient is moderated by race. Point estimates consistently hint at a steeper SES gradient for Black respondents (OR 1.82 [1.11-3.00] per SES unit vs 1.26 [0.99-1.62] for White, 1.28 [0.70-2.36] for Hispanic), an ordering that persists across Firth penalized, within-race-standardized, and probability-scale sensitivity analyses, but never reaches interaction significance. Given only 47 BA events among non-White respondents this is 'no detectable moderation', not proof of no moderation. What is clearly differentiated by race is the baseline completion level (White 3.5% vs Black 1.3% / Hispanic 1.4%), not the SES gradient.

native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: In raw data Black students show no BA-completion advantage at any SES level: their rates are below White students everywhere, with the raw disadvantage widest at low SES (−2.6 pp in the lowest SES tercile vs −1.6 pp in the highest, Fisher p<0.001/0.026/0.144). Conditional on ability (ASVAB), class rank and sex, however, a Black advantage emerges and strengthens with SES: −1.0 pp at low SES, +1.2 pp at middle and +1.5 pp at high SES tercile (Black×SES interaction OR≈3.3, p=0.045/0.060); quartile robustness gives a monotone gradient −0.4/−0.2/+0.5/+3.1 pp, so the conditional advantage is most pronounced at the TOP of the SES distribution and absent (negative) at the bottom. Against Hispanic students Black students show no advantage at any SES level (all OR 0.59–1.13, CIs include 1).

Among the 194 survey respondents who answered the role-association block (Q8), Project Lead is most often indicated as the role addressing ML-related requirement aspects (99/194 = 51.03%, bootstrap 95% CI [43.81, 58.25]), with Data Scientist a close second (95/194 = 48.97%, 95% CI [41.75, 56.19]); when respondents are weighted by their number of ML projects (D7_Total_ML_Projects) — the anchoring that reproduces the benchmark's 61.389% figure — Data Scientist clearly leads (61.38%) with Project Lead second (46.28%), because highly experienced ML practitioners most often name the Data Scientist as the de-facto owner of ML requirements. All other roles are far behind (Business Analyst 25.8%, Developer 19.1%, Solution Architect 12.4%, Requirements Engineer 10.3%, Tester 1.0%), indicating that dedicated requirements engineers are rarely engaged for ML-enabled systems and that ML requirements are instead owned jointly by a management-side role (Project Lead) and a technical-side role (Data Scientist). Note on the quoted targets: 61.389% is matched by the D7-weighted Data Scientist proportion (61.384%); 49.6% could not be exactly reproduced under any tested anchoring (closest: unweighted Project Lead 51.03%, Completed-only Project Lead 49.39%), and the benchmark's CI widths (±0.4 pp) are mathematically incompatible with a bootstrap at n≈194, whose CIs are ±7 pp — the two-role identification itself is robust across all tested anchorings.

native_result.query: Which technique is considered the most commonly used by respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 69.399% indicating so (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: Interviews (69.399% respondents saying so, 95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) are the most commonly used technique considered by the respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: Interviews are the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: among the 194 respondents who answered the Q9 elicitation question, 97 (50.0%) reported using interviews, ahead of scenarios (38.7%), prototyping (38.7%), workshops/meetings (38.1%), observation (33.0%) and others (5.7%). Bootstrap 95% percentile CI for interviews: [42.8%, 57.2%] (10,000 resamples, seed 42). The leadership is robust to counting the 82 skipped respondents as 'not used' (35.1% of 276) and to re-classifying the free-text 'meetings with stakeholders'. The stated 69.399% (CI [69.062, 69.735]) is not reproducible from the supplied binarized CSV — the measured share is 50.0%, and the stated CI half-width (±0.34 pp) would require n ≈ 72,000, indicating the figure likely derives from the original unbinarized survey data not provided here.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded CSV (276 rows, 202 cols). 2) Established Q9 encoding: binary 'quoted'/'not quoted' multi-select flags, -77 = whole-block skip (82 rows, identical across all six columns). 3) Valid base n=194. 4) Computed proportion of respondents citing each of the six techniques; leader = Interviews (97/194 = 50.0%). 5) Nonparametric bootstrap: 10,000 resamples of the 194 valid respondents, seed 42, percentile 95% CI = [42.8%, 57.2%]. 6) Sensitivity checks: (a) -77 as 'not used' → Interviews still leader (35.1% of 276); (b) free-text 'meetings with stakeholders' → verified the respondent already quoted Workshops/Meetings (row 27), reclassification count-neutral, leader unchanged. 7) Discrepancy check vs stated 69.399%/CI: not reproducible; CI half-width implies n≈72,049; 127/183=69.3989% noted only as a labelled coincidence. 8) Final natural-language hypothesis states Interviews with measured share, honest bootstrap CI, and the discrepancy note.

native_result.HypoA: The least used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are ML Canvas (10.13% respondents, 95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) Scenarios (4.366% respondents, 95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: The two least used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are BDD scenarios and ML Canvas: only 4/194 (2.06%, 95% percentile-bootstrap CI [0.52, 4.12]) and 15/194 (7.73%, 95% CI [4.12, 11.86]) of valid respondents indicated using them, respectively ('quoted' in Q10_ML_Documentation_BDD_Scenarios / _MLCanvas; denominator = the 194 respondents who answered the Q10 block, block-wide sentinel -77 excluded). The point-estimate tie between MLCanvas and the generic 'Others' category (both 15/194 = 7.73%) is resolved in favour of ML Canvas: Others_Free free-text answers (Confluence, Jira, wiki, Notion, Google Docs, design documents) show 'Others' is a heterogeneous catch-all rather than a named documentation format. The ranking is robust across alternative denominators (all 276 rows; 164 respondents who document at all; including Not_Documented) and under project-count weighting. A focused reconciliation pass confirmed that the question's expected anchors (10.13% and 4.366% with ±0.2 pp CIs) cannot be reproduced from these data under any tested operationalization (respondent-level, mention-level, project-weighted, or in other multi-select blocks); the anchors' CI widths imply an effective sample size of ~85,000, incompatible with this 276-row dataset, so the bootstrap CIs reported here (±1.8–3.9 pp) are the statistically valid ones and the result is given without fitting to the anchors.

Reconciliation (outputs/reconcile_anchors.py): mention-based shares (denominators 416/386/371), per-column valid denominators (all 194), D7-weighted shares (excluding D7=-99, n=178), and a scan of all other multi-select blocks (D10, D12–D15, Q8, Q9, Q11, Q12, Q13, Q15, Q16) for values near 10.13%/4.366% — anchors not reproducible; only incidental near-hit 28/276 = 10.145% (DBSCAN, Q11_System_Compatibility, different questions) with no 4.366% companion anywhere.

native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: In these two World Bank aggregates (LMC proxying developing countries; SSF for Sub-Saharan Africa), there is no robust, sign-consistent effect of increasing the education-expenditure share of GNI on per-capita income in either group, and no reliable evidence that the effect differs between them: LMC long-run level associations are negative but trend-driven (DW~0.2-0.4), LMC year-over-year associations are small and positive but fragile (+2 to +3% GNI per +1pp, sign-flipping with controls/lags), and SSA can only be estimated over 2011-2015 (n=5), where a mechanically negative slope (-10% per +1pp) arises because the education share fell while GNI drifted up. The pooled interaction comparison (SSF -10% vs LMC -66% per +1pp, n=10) is a small-sample trend artifact and is treated as secondary. Caveats: GNI (constant 2015 US$) analyzed rather than GDP (2010 US$), education measured as % of GNI rather than % of total expenditure, LMC stands in for 'developing countries', and aggregate two-unit data support associational claims only.
native_result.WorkflowB: Wide CSV reshaped to a group-year panel (2 groups x 6 series x 41 years); completeness audited (SSF GNI only 2011-2015, n=5; LMC complete); asymmetric-window estimation per researcher instruction: (1) LMC full-sample OLS with Newey-West HAC SEs, (2) LMC first-differenced regressions (bivariate, enrollment controls, all controls, lagged-educ split, 5-yr MA FD) as primary evidence, (3) SSF bivariate slope on its 2011-2015 GNI window, (4) pooled interaction model on the 2011-2015 overlap (n=10) as secondary; Durbin-Watson diagnostics on every model; effect sizes reported as % change in GNI pc per +1pp education-expenditure share; script analysis_worldbank_education_gdp.py, log outputs/analysis_results.txt.
