native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In NLSY79, higher time preference (present-oriented financial behavior: dissaving, lower net savings flow, lower accumulated wealth) is associated with modestly higher BMI: dissavers in 1989 had ~0.26 BMI units higher BMI in 1989 (+0.45 vs savers when 'no savings' is modeled separately; 'no savings' group +0.54), each savings-flow quintile of higher saving is associated with -0.19 BMI units, and dissaving predicts BMI gain 1981-1989 (+0.20, p=0.028); obesity odds ratio 1.17 (p=0.058). Wealth accumulation 1985-1990 shows no association (p=0.71) while 1996 wealth level is weakly protective (-0.030, p=0.021). native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: In the 17th century BCE (bin starting 1700 BCE; 1700–1601 BCE), the diversity of pottery form collapsed (Z: +0.74 → −1.13, ΔZ = −1.87, the largest negative form-slope in the 4300–500 BCE record) while the diversity of pottery decoration simultaneously increased (Z: −0.48 → +0.97, ΔZ = +1.45, a top-percentile positive decoration-slope), and this anti-phase transition is the only century in the entire record where both conditions coincide in the same 100-year bin under empirically fixed 5%/95% slope thresholds; the new regime then persisted for ~10 centuries (form flat at −1.13, decoration at +0.97/+1.53).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded capital.csv (decimal=','), mapped BCE→CE=-BCE and verified numeric identity with time_series_data.csv raw PotteryForm/PotteryDecoration on all 37 overlapping century bins (max diff 0.0). 2) Computed century-to-century slopes dZ (newer minus older) on the raw 100-yr values (primary). 3) Fixed collapse/increase thresholds as the 5th/95th percentiles of the empirical slope distributions before inspecting any result. 4) Detected bins satisfying both conditions in the same century (unique: 1700 BCE) plus ±100-yr sensitivity and 100-yr-rolling-mean confirmation on the annual _inter series (both criteria also met; Spearman corr of slopes ~0.57–0.58). 5) Exported full evidence table (slope_evidence_table.csv) and the executed script (analysis_pottery.py).

native_result.HypoA: Symbolic capital components such as house size, the number of daggers, and hatchets/swords are characterized by negative values on the first principal component (PC1) and exhibit a wide distribution of values on the second principal component (PC2). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: En la PCA sobre formas de capital en cortes de 100 años (PC1=30.3%, PC2=19.5%), el capital simbólico (ZAxtSchwert +0.30, ZDolch +0.27, Zhausgr +0.23) carga positiva y moderadamente en PC1, covariando con el polo de prestigio/display (cobre-oro +0.41, cerámica decorada +0.38, depósitos +0.34, monumentos +0.20/+0.24) y opuesto a las formas utilitarias (forma cerámica −0.35, hachas-celtas −0.24, ámbar −0.24); los scores de PC1 pasan de fuertemente negativos en EN/MN/SG (≈−1.8 a −1.1) a fuertemente positivos en OBA/YBA (máximo +4.5 en 1100 a.C.), de modo que el capital simbólico se intensifica hacia la Edad del Bronce Final. native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: La prevalencia de plantas no nativas introducidas por jardinería varía fuertemente según el hábitat: es máxima en humedales, costas y bosques (proporción de registros de jardinería ~0,55-1,00; OR ajustados ~2,4-2,6 vs urbano) y mínima en cultivos y afloramientos rocosos (~0-0,19; OR ~0,31), con hábitats urbanos y riparianos intermedios (~0,30-0,37). El patrón no se explica por la urbanización local ni por la elevación tras el ajuste, y se amplifica porque la jardinería pasó del 17% de las introducciones (antes de 1500) al 75% (1985-2019), concentrando los no nativos recientes en los hábitats más receptivos a propágulos ornamentales.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga y verificación de integridad (632 parcelas, 0 duplicados, n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo=n.total en todas; árbol con 81 tips coincidentes con phylo.tip.label). 2) Descriptivos por hábitat: prevalencia n.gard/n.total y riqueza absoluta por parcela con IC bootstrap (5000 remuestreos). 3) Chi² hábitat×vía (75,2, df=18, p=5,8e-9, V=0,28) con residuos estandarizados. 4) VIF iterativo: annual.temperature eliminada (VIF 21,7; r=-0,96 con elevación). 5) Modelo de dos componentes: (a) GLM binomial HC3 para presencia de no-nativas (gestiona las 441 parcelas sin no-nativas), (b) GLM binomial HC3 para la fracción de jardinería (betabinomial MLE convergió a rho=0,002 = sin sobredispersión; chi²/df=1,01; opción documentada). 6) Sensibilidad con coberturas 1956/1993 y cambios progresivo/regresivo: orden de hábitats estable. 7) Contexto temporal (Gardening 0,17→0,75 entre pre-1500 y 1985-2019) y de rasgos de especies. Sustituciones de paquetes: sin R/glmmTMB -> betabinomial vía MLE scipy + GLM statsmodels HC3; sin Biopython -> parser Newick propio; sin matplotlib.

sub_hypo.text: La jardinería pasó del 17% de las introducciones de plantas no nativas antes de 1500 al 75% en 1985–2019, amplificando el patrón de concentración de no nativas recientes en hábitats receptivos a propágulos ornamentales.
sub_hypo.context: Tendencias temporales de las vías de introducción de flora no nativa en Cataluña, comparando antes de 1500 con 1985–2019, vinculadas en la hipótesis al patrón por hábitat observado en Barcelona.
sub_hypo.relations: La proporción de introducciones correspondiente a Gardening aumenta de 0,17 a 0,75 entre ambos períodos. La hipótesis plantea que este aumento amplifica la concentración de no nativas recientes en los hábitats más receptivos a propágulos ornamentales.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: La prevalencia de plantas no nativas introducidas por jardinería varía fuertemente según el hábitat: es máxima en humedales, costas y bosques (proporción de registros de jardinería ~0,55-1,00; OR ajustados ~2,4-2,6 vs urbano) y mínima en cultivos y afloramientos rocosos (~0-0,19; OR ~0,31), con hábitats urbanos y riparianos intermedios (~0,30-0,37). El patrón no se explica por la urbanización local ni por la elevación tras el ajuste, y se amplifica porque la jardinería pasó del 17% de las introducciones (antes de 1500) al 75% (1985-2019), concentrando los no nativos recientes en los hábitats más receptivos a propágulos ornamentales.

native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted a specific type of plant invasion in the scenario of consolidated, spatially extensive urbanization (the 'Urban' habitat and high urban cover persisting since before 1956, best detected at the 500 m neighbourhood buffer, strengthening through 1993–2009). Under this scenario, invasions are dominated by UNINTENTIONALLY introduced annual ruderal herbs of low stature and broad invaded niche — mainly Asteraceae and Amaranthaceae (Erigeron/Conyza spp., Amaranthus retroflexus, Symphyotrichum squamatum, Xanthium spp.) — rather than by ornamental garden escapes, which are predominantly perennial/woody (Robinia pseudoacacia, Pittosporum tobira, Lonicera japonica). New progressive urban/cropland expansion does not (yet) host these unintentional invaders; the effect belongs to long-established urban landscapes. The pathway-specific invasion types are phylogenetically structured (adjacent tree tips share pathway more than expected by chance, p=0.008).

native_result.query: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promotes the invasion of introduced plants mainly by filtering which plant types establish: invasion occurrence rises steeply with urbanization (8.6% of parcels with invaders in the lowest urban-cover tercile vs 65.2% in the highest, 500 m buffer), but this is largely mediated by habitat type (urban-habitat plots 83% invaded vs <7% in forests/scrub; habitat LRT p~1e-15). Within invaded plots, urbanization shifts composition of the invading flora: unintentionally introduced annual herbs with the broadest invaded niches increase their share (54%→67% from low to high urban tercile), while AgriForest introductions decline sharply (8%→2%, p=0.017) and gardening-introduced woody species decline mildly (38%→32%; gardening IRR=0.43, p=0.043). Overall invasion success is higher for unintentionally introduced species (+9.7 invaded plots vs gardening, p=0.009), species with broader invaded niche breadth (p=0.047) and longer residence time (p=0.03); and because the regional introduction pool is increasingly gardening-sourced (17% before 1500 → 75% in 1985-2019), the urban filter increasingly acts on an ornamental-dominated pool, favouring its ruderal, unintentionally-spread component.

Overall invasion success is higher for unintentionally introduced species (+9.7 invaded plots vs gardening, p=0.009), species with broader invaded niche breadth (p=0.047) and longer residence time (p=0.03); and because the regional introduction pool is increasingly gardening-sourced (17% before 1500 → 75% in 1985-2019), the urban filter increasingly acts on an ornamental-dominated pool, favouring its ruderal, unintentionally-spread component.

P0||G0.query: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?
P0||G0.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
P0||G0.HypoB: Urban land use promotes the invasion of introduced plants mainly by filtering which plant types establish: invasion occurrence rises steeply with urbanization (8.6% of parcels with invaders in the lowest urban-cover tercile vs 65.2% in the highest, 500 m buffer), but this is largely mediated by habitat type (urban-habitat plots 83% invaded vs <7% in forests/scrub; habitat LRT p~1e-15). Within invaded plots, urbanization shifts composition of the invading flora: unintentionally introduced annual herbs with the broadest invaded niches increase their share (54%→67% from low to high urban tercile), while AgriForest introductions decline sharply (8%→2%, p=0.017) and gardening-introduced woody species decline mildly (38%→32%; gardening IRR=0.43, p=0.043). Overall invasion success is higher for unintentionally introduced species (+9.7 invaded plots vs gardening, p=0.009), species with broader invaded niche breadth (p=0.047) and longer residence time (p=0.03); and because the regional introduction pool is increasingly gardening-sourced (17% before 1500 → 75% in 1985-2019), the urban filter increasingly acts on an ornamental-dominated pool, favouring its ruderal, unintentionally-spread component.
P0||G0.WorkflowB: 1) Data inspection and sanity checks (dimensions, NAs, phylo tip matching 77/81, n.total=rowwise sum verified). 2) Plot-level (invaded_niche_pathways.csv, 632 plots): logistic GLM for presence of invaders with urban cover 2009/1956 + cropland 2009 (500 m main; 50 m and 1000 m sensitivity), covariates habitat/elevation/climate/distances; pathway-specific conditional Poisson GLMs (HC1) for n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo given n.total>0; composition of invaders across urbanization terciles with chi-square tests and Spearman trend; Moran-like residual autocorrelation check. 3) Species-level (invasion_success_pathways.csv, 81 species): pathway x growth.form cross-tab (chi-square), OLS of number of invaded plots on pathway x growth.form + log residence time + height with family-clustered SEs (phylogeny tools unavailable in environment), Kruskal-Wallis for niche breadth. 4) Temporal context from contingency table. 5) Supplementary: reduced models without habitat, overdispersion check, collinearity of land-change dummies, Urban-habitat-specific correlation. Tools: pandas 3.0.2, numpy, scipy 1.16.0, statsmodels 0.14.6.

Question: For both HypoA and HypoB, what are the different variables found in the hypotheses?         Return your answer as a JSON object in the following format:
        ```json
        {{
        "sizeA": num of variables used in HypoA
        "sizeB": num of variables used in HypoB
        "intersection": num of variables common in HypoA and HypoB. Use *fuzzy matching* to determine intersection, accounting for paraphrases or slightly different surface forms
        "explanation": a short text explanation about the variables
        }}```
        Answer:

score.explanation: HypoA uses urban land cover, invasion level, and introduction pathway (gardening versus unintentional). HypoB uses urban land cover, invasion occurrence, habitat type, introduction pathway, growth form, invaded niche breadth, residence time, number of invaded plots, introduction period, introduction-pool proportions, and pathway shares within invaded plots. Both share urban land cover, introduction pathway, and invasion level, fuzzy-matched to HypoB's invasion outcomes. Buffer sizes, statistical estimates, and p-values are not counted as separate variables.

Question: Does HypoB exhibit the same relation as HypoA?
        Compare using following example hierarchy of relationships (based on specificity):         "there exists a relationship" > "positive relationship" > "positive AND (linear OR quadratic)" > "positive AND linear".
        Options: A) very similar B) similar but general than HypoA C) different
        Return your answer as a JSON object in the following format:
        ```json
        {{
        "answer": one of the options from A) very similar B) similar but general than HypoA C) different
        "explanation": a short text explanation about the relationship comparison
        }}```
        Answer:
rel.answer: {"answer":"A) very similar","explanation":"Both hypotheses describe urban land use as disadvantaging gardening introductions relative to unintentional introductions. HypoB makes this relation more specific: gardening plants decline in share and have a negative urbanization association, while unintentionally introduced plants increase in share. Its additional claim that overall invasion rises with urbanization does not contradict this pathway-specific relation."}

native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. native_result.HypoB: Original-study effect sizes exceed replication effect sizes in all three domains (Social, Cognitive, Economics). Discipline is confounded with replication project, yet the pattern holds in both rpp and ee; excluding 18 sign-inverted pairs preserves conclusions; variance-weighted analysis weakens Economics evidence (p=0.69), so inflation is best established for Social and Cognitive.

native_result.query: What is the average length of original papers in Experimental Economics and that in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: Studies in Experimental Economics tend to have longer original papers compared to Psychology. The average length of original papers in Experimental Economics is 28 pages, whereas in Psychology, the average is 11 pages.
native_result.HypoB: Original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than original papers in Psychology: the average length is about 28 pages (mean 28.0, median 27.5, SD 7.4, range 16–45; n=18) for Experimental Economics originals versus about 11 pages (mean 11.2, median 9, SD 6.4, range 1–31; n=95 unique papers) for Psychology originals in the Reproducibility Project — a difference of roughly 17 pages, i.e., economics originals average ~2.5× the length of psychology originals.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded the 927x57 meta-regression study dataset; verified length has no missing values and is constant within each study id; took project=='ee' (18 papers, no duplicates) and project=='rpp' (97 rows, 95 unique titles) as Experimental Economics and Psychology respectively; computed article-level means/medians/SDs/ranges with rpp deduplicated by title (primary, n=95) and row-level (check, n=97); confirmed deduplication shifts the rpp mean by only 0.01 pages; concluded ee originals average ~28 pages vs ~11 pages for rpp (difference ≈17 pages, ratio ≈2.5×). Script: analysis/avg_length_ee_vs_rpp.py; output: analysis/avg_length_ee_vs_rpp_output.txt.

native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration is associated with a near-complete stall — and, for those who started with some wealth, a reversal — of wealth accumulation, with the setback scaling with initial socioeconomic position (1985 wealth terciles as income proxy). In the lowest tercile (1985 median wealth ≈ $0), ever-jailed respondents remain pinned at $0 median wealth through 1996, capturing only ~30% of the wealth growth of non-jailed peers ($6,077 vs $20,203 winsorized mean change). In the middle tercile their median wealth change by 1996 is negative (−$1,000 vs +$6,231 for non-jailed); in the highest tercile it is strongly negative (−$5,800 vs +$8,825), i.e., jailed respondents in the top tercile end 1996 with LESS wealth than they had in 1985. The jailed-vs-never-jailed wealth gap widens monotonically with initial wealth (≈$14K, $28K, $52K in winsorized mean 1985→1996 change; jailed×top-tercile OLS interaction −$35.2K, p=0.017). So the dollar and proportional wealth setback is largest for Black individuals who started mid-to-high wealth, while the poorest third are locked out of accumulation entirely (median wealth stuck at $0). Descriptive association, not causal: baseline wealth differences, an overlapping 1985–1994 treatment window, and a coarse composite wealth measure limit interpretation.

native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality between white males and females vanished at the median (male/female median ratio moved from 0.776 to 1.008), but convergence happened downward: medians fell for both sexes (males -43%, females -56%) while means rose (~+49% and +29%) and the 90th percentile grew ~55%, roughly tripling the p90/p50 ratio within each group (~12-14 to ~37-38). Within-group inequality therefore increased sharply in the lower half (mean/median ratio ~5 to ~15), although the Gini stayed nearly constant (~0.78-0.80), indicating the change was concentrated at the bottom mass and upper tail. This finding is conditional on the apparent jump in zero-wealth share (~20-26% in 1990 to ~42-43% in 1996), a possible 1996 coding artifact: excluding zeros, relative within-group inequality instead decreases (p90/p50 ~6 to ~4; Gini ~0.71 to ~0.62-0.64) and medians rise. Results are robust to p1-p99 winsorization and to excluding negative values (treated as valid net debts in the base analysis; extreme value -866,400 documented). All figures are in current dollars; inflation adjustment (~22% 1990->1996) would deepen the real median decline but does not change the scale-invariant inequality ratios.

Within-group inequality therefore increased sharply in the lower half (mean/median ratio ~5 to ~15), although the Gini stayed nearly constant (~0.78-0.80), indicating the change was concentrated at the bottom mass and upper tail. This finding is conditional on the apparent jump in zero-wealth share (~20-26% in 1990 to ~42-43% in 1996), a possible 1996 coding artifact: excluding zeros, relative within-group inequality instead decreases (p90/p50 ~6 to ~4; Gini ~0.71 to ~0.62-0.64) and medians rise. Results are robust to p1-p99 winsorization and to excluding negative values (treated as valid net debts in the base analysis; extreme value -866,400 documented). All figures are in current dollars; inflation adjustment (~22% 1990->1996) would deepen the real median decline but does not change the scale-invariant inequality ratios.

native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: En los tres años analizados (1985, 1990 y 1996), las personas con antecedentes de encarcelamiento (ever_jailed=1, encarcelado entre 1985 y 1994) tienen una riqueza compuesta significativamente menor que quienes no los tienen, tras ajustar por raza y sexo: la brecha ajustada es de -9.441 dólares en 1985, -35.394 en 1990 y -60.911 en 1996 (todos los p ajustados Holm < 1e-6; Mann-Whitney concordante). The sparse Firth BA (grade>=16) models replicate this directional pattern with very wide uncertainty.

sub_hypo.text: Childhood SES is the dominant moderator of the racial education gap: Black students' educational disadvantage is concentrated at low SES and attenuates as SES rises.

sub_hypo.context: Participantes del NLSY79; análisis limitado a las tres olas de riqueza de 1985, 1990 y 1996, en dólares nominales. Las medianas por cohorte y año conservan ceros y valores negativos, tratados como riqueza genuina; se realiza una sensibilidad secundaria excluyendo negativos. La interpretación está condicionada por la atrición diferencial, incluida una no respuesta del 52.6% en la cohorte no-negra no-hispana en 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: La mediana de riqueza de la cohorte no-negra no-hispana supera consistentemente las medianas negra e hispana en las tres olas. En 1985, sus $3,500 equivalen a 2.2 veces la mediana negra ($1,600) y 7 veces la hispana ($500); en 1996, sus $42,600 equivalen a 4.3 veces la negra ($9,800) y 16.6 veces la hispana ($2,562). Entre ambos extremos, la brecha frente a negros aumenta de $1,900 a $32,800 y frente a hispanos de $3,000 a $40,038.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Entre 1985 y 1996, los individuos no-negros no-hispánicos (proxy de individuos blancos, supuesto declarado) poseen consistentemente una riqueza familiar neta mediana muy superior a la de individuos negros e hispanos, y la brecha se amplía: en 1985 la mediana blanca-proxy ($3,500) era 2.2× la negra ($1,600) y 7× la hispana ($500); en 1996 ($42,600) era 4.3× la negra ($9,800) y 16.6× la hispana ($2,562). Las brechas en dólares crecieron de $1,900 a $32,800 (frente a negros) y de $3,000 a $40,038 (frente a hispanos). Interpretación condicionada por: solo tres olas de riqueza (1985/1990/1996), cifras nominales, y atrición diferencial (no respuesta del 52.6% en la cohorte 3 en 1996).

native_result.query: Is the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines of the individual?
native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: In the NLS data, the SES-to-BA-completion relationship is significantly moderated by race (LR chi2=9.57, df=2, p=0.008): a one-SD increase in SES multiplies the odds of BA completion by ~2.7 for Black respondents (95% CI 1.68-4.20), ~2.0 for Hispanic respondents (1.16-3.32), but only ~1.24 for White respondents (1.02-1.51). White respondents complete the BA at higher absolute rates at every SES level (3.1%->3.8% vs Black 0.4%->2.2%, Hispanic 0.8%->3.1%), yet their odds are far less SES-sensitive (SES x White OR=0.47, p=0.003), producing a crossover at high SES. Adjusting for academic performance (ASVAB composite, class percentile), family size and sex halves the White contrast (b: -0.76 -> -0.37, n.s.) while the Black gradient remains the steepest (OR=1.83, p=0.018), indicating partial mediation through academic resources. Hypothesis: socioeconomic status is a substantially stronger predictor of college-degree completion for Black and Hispanic youth than for White youth, whose completion is comparatively high and largely insensitive to family SES; part of this racial difference in SES sensitivity reflects differential academic-resource endowments.

(4) Nested logistic models: M1 (SES + race dummies), M2 (+ SES x race interaction), M3 (+ ASVAB composite, class percentile, family size, sex; interpreted as partial mediation/decomposition), M4 (triple SES x race x sex, n.s.). (5) LR test of the interaction block; race-specific SES ORs via delta-method variances. (6) Robustness: LPM with HC1 errors, SES-tertile logit, L2-penalized logit (direction check under sparse events), predicted-probability curves. All models converged; only 236 positive events (2.69% base rate).

native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: En NLSY79, mayor impaciencia (sacar dinero de los ahorros o no tener ahorros en 1989, frente a poner dinero) se asocia con mayor BMI medido en 1992 (y 1989 en sensibilidad): gradiente monótono de ~1,5 puntos de BMI entre 'sin ahorros' (26,89) y 'puso dinero' (25,36), que persiste tras ajustar por sexo, raza/etnia, edad, educación, ingreso y patrimonio (β ordinal = −0,34 BMI/nivel, p<1e-7). Los datos APOYAN la dirección 'mayor impaciencia → mayor BMI', pero la asociación es correlacional, de magnitud modesta, y solo es significativa con el proxy ordinal o logarítmico, no con el flujo bruto de dólares estandarizado.
native_result.WorkflowB: Carga de nls_raw.csv (12.686×61); conversión altura 1981 pies+pulgadas→pulgadas; pesos libras→kg con filtro [50,450] lb (11 excluidos); flujo neto de ahorro 1989 = (puesto − sacado) con ceros estructurales por patrón de salto y top-codes recodificados; proxy ordinal (0 sin ahorros … 3 puso dinero); indicador JAIL (residencia=5, 1981–1996, 4,52%); BMI = kg/m² con altura 1985+peso 1992 (principal, n=8.544) y altura 1981+peso 1989 (sensibilidad, n=10.199); comparación por terciles (rank-based), OLS con HC3 y controles sexo/raza/edad/educación/ingreso (± patrimonio 1985/1990), flujo estandarizado y por desviación estándar, n reportado por especificación; sensibilidades: log-flujo, winsorizado p99, exclusión de JAIL.

sub_hypo.text: En NLSY79, mayor impaciencia, representada por sacar dinero de los ahorros o no tener ahorros en 1989 frente a poner dinero, se asocia con mayor BMI en 1992, con BMI de 1989 como sensibilidad. El gradiente es monótono: 26,89 entre quienes no tenían ahorros frente a 25,36 entre quienes pusieron dinero, una diferencia aproximada de 1,5 puntos. La asociación persiste al ajustar por sexo, raza/etnia, edad, educación, ingreso y patrimonio: β ordinal = −0,34 puntos de BMI por nivel, p<1e-7. Es una asociación correlacional y modesta, significativa con el proxy ordinal o logarítmico, pero no con el flujo bruto de dólares estandarizado.
sub_hypo.context: Participantes de NLSY79 con datos disponibles por especificación. Análisis principal: BMI calculado con altura de 1985 y peso de 1992 (n=8.544); sensibilidad: altura de 1981 y peso de 1989 (n=10.199). Se filtraron los pesos al intervalo [50,450] lb, excluyendo 11 observaciones. Las sensibilidades incluyeron flujo logarítmico, winsorización p99 y exclusión de participantes con residencia JAIL (código 5) en 1981–1996.

sub_hypo.relations: Mayor impaciencia se asocia con mayor BMI; equivalentemente, niveles ordinales más altos de ahorro se asocian con menor BMI. Gradiente monótono de 26,89 a 25,36 entre sin ahorros y puso dinero. En OLS con errores HC3 y controles por sexo, raza/etnia, edad, educación, ingreso y patrimonio, β ordinal = −0,34 BMI/nivel (p<1e-7). La significación depende de la operacionalización: presente con el proxy ordinal o logarítmico, ausente con el flujo bruto de dólares estandarizado. La relación es correlacional, no causal, y de magnitud modesta.
